speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: And, no, it is not which football team they support for the World Cup finals!

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: It is the fact that Dr Ng Eng Hen, Deputy Prime Ministers Mr Teo Chee Hean as well as Mr Tharman Shanmugaratnam, have all "cut their teeth" in the Ministry of Education (MOE), they have led, enabled and elevated this Ministry.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: Long before any call for greater equality in the education system, Minister Heng asked that "Every student should be an engaged learner", regardless of background or ability.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: He said that to support this, we will need: "Every teacher to be a caring educator"; "every parent, a supportive partner".

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: And, of course, his trademark quotation, "Every School, a Good School"!

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: Today, our Motion paints a portrait of students, educators, schools and parents.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: It questions the assumptions about individual stakeholders and system designers collectively, both bear responsibility to improve the future of education in Singapore.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: Improvements that ensure accessible, inclusive and lifelong education for all learners.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: We speak to this House, Mr Speaker, as academics, educators, professionals, business persons and parents keenly interested in the future of Singapore's education system.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: We, ourselves, are Singaporeans who have benefited from a world-class education system and our education system is that.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: But we also know that the most important lessons that you learn is to cherish the ability to give back to society whenever you can; to always be independent-minded, ever ready to question the status quo for the sake of progress and ready to refine the methods that have worked in the past but may not be so productive today or may even be outmoded.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: Here is a snapshot, Mr Speaker, of what we will cover in this Motion.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin will highlight the importance of recognising the talents of every student.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: She will suggest ways to refine how assessments are conducted in primary and secondary schools, even taking a leaf, perhaps, from what preschools are currently doing.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: Mr Louis Ng will further ask that performance-based rankings of teachers should be reviewed.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: He will also ask that preschool and lower primary students should be encouraged to play and explore and that we should not be overly focused on academic content at this formative early stage of education.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: Ms Chia Yong Yong and Ms Rahayu Mahzam will ask that special education schools and mainstream primary and secondary schools be encouraged to work together to ensure that students with special needs are integrated in settings that are appropriate and that meet their needs.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: Mr Azmoon Ahmad will propose ways to ensure social mobility and national integration are best preserved as we go forward.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: He will also suggest that we should look into multiple strategies, not the one-size-fits-all formula.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: Prof Randolph Tan will ask that we build on the strengths of the current system and anticipate the challenges of technological disruption with effective and future-ready policies that are already being deployed in other comparable jurisdictions.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: Ms K Thanaletchimi similarly will ask if our Institutes of Higher Learning (IHLs) have matched the new opportunities that have arisen and whether old barometers of success come with risks and may not always be applicable anymore.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: And Mr Ganesh Rajaram will share why sports education and Direct School Admission (DSA) should be better insulated from tuition and mismanaged expectations from coaches and parents alike.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: I have three points, Mr Speaker, in my own speech.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: The first is about tuition and false advertising.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: I have put together a photo collage which Mr Speaker has kindly reminded that it may be too much to actually be shown up.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: But this collage is something that I collected from just a visit to Coronation Plaza which is often frequented by parents and students alike from all the primary and secondary schools in that area in Bukit Timah, a stone's throw away from the top primary and secondary schools.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: They suggest that you will be guaranteed a PSLE score of 279, much higher than I had ever got, if you would just move to this particular tuition agency.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: They suggest that they have 91% proven track record of As and A-stars.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: Yet, does this necessarily mean that Singaporean students are ready for the brave new world of tomorrow?

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: Or does it only suggest that we are exam-smart as a nation?

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: After all, companies from countries that do very well PISA-wise barely feature in other rankings for business, for companies, of the Top 25 most successful companies, as an example, in Forbes.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: So, I ask, what can or should we do differently?

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: Are there plans for a total systems review, much like the Goh Report of the past?

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: Such a review could aim to change the attitudes of parents, teachers and students towards examinations and grades.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: But the best way to do so is for all our schools and IHLs to give due weightage to aptitude testing – not just grades, but what is the aptitude of each student – and that is very much at the core of today's Motion.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: And they must "never become self-perpetuating, closed circles", as the Prime Minister noted in this House in May.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: Second, let me say a bit more about neighbourhood primary schools and Raffles Institution (RI).

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: Let us never forget the contributions of neighbourhood primary school teachers.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: My colleagues and I have separately spoken to a few and the stories of one has rung true with me.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: Mr Kumaran Veera is the Head of Department at Concord Primary School in Chua Chu Kang.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: He teaches Primary 5 and Primary 6 students.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: Concord Primary School has consistently improved over the years because of him and his colleagues and its Applied Learning and Learning for Life programmes (APL and LLP).

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: But what made me sit up when speaking to Mr Kumaran and his colleagues were the stories that they had beyond just the rankings, beyond just the ALP and LLP.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: Kumaran's stories are not of children who are bored in class because of too much tuition.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: They are stories of bright girls and boys who sit at the back of the class and, sometimes, do not even come to school because parents do not encourage them to turn up at school.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: Stories of him and others visiting the houses of such students and using tough love, Mr Speaker, to encourage these students to attend school and tough love on the parents as well to send their children to school.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: It helps that Mr Kumaran is more than six feet tall and is built like a discipline master should be.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: But I congratulate every neighbourhood primary school like Concord that continues to make a difference.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: Like Kumaran, I am proud to come from a neighbourhood primary school myself.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: Contrary to its name, Princess Elizabeth Primary School has nothing to do with the United Kingdom!

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: It is named after a road which is based in Bukit Batok right now.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: It used to be Hillview, but now it is Bukit Batok.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: After the PSLE, I was fortunate to get a place in RI.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: And let me say a few words about RI.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: Those four years were the most blissful years of a kid's education.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: RI has held itself up as the best school, but not because it has always put itself up to be that, but because none of us came from a feeder primary school, Mr Speaker.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: No one dared to think, when they entered RI in Secondary 1, that they were the best in the class, a subject or a sport because we had no idea who might be better than you; we were all just equals coming there.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: Your path was never paved for you; you worked hard to earn your own reputation.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: My schoolmates could not have been from more diverse backgrounds or sensibilities.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: I was thus concerned when the Prime Minister raised in May that diversity had become an issue in RI.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: And I am happy to report that after speaking to Vice Principals and teachers at RI, they have tried to take some swift action to combat this perception.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: RI has established a scholarship and mentorship programme for Primary 5 and Primary 6 students from across the country.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: I spoke to Mrs Theresa Lai, a Vice Principal, who hopes that, through this mentorship and scholarship programmes, RI can play a part in the social mobility of these students with both financial support and also through "old school", "older brother/older sister" mentorship, where you have Secondary 1 and Secondary 2 students actually going to meet their counterparts, or their juniors in primary school to encourage them.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: Although the mentors provide academic support, the larger idea is to work with these nine- and 10-year-olds in primary school to deal with the socio-emotional stresses and what leadership skills actually involve.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: RI has also engaged the principals and teachers from primary schools to see how they can better support these students.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: This year, for example, the school had almost 60 primary schools represented at its yearly dialogue sessions.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: Through these engagement efforts, RI, as a school, tries to dispel the notion that it is an exclusive educational institution; it is not only for the bright children from	wealthy backgrounds.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: It is a tough journey, partly because that is the assumption that many of us have, even those of us who have gone to the school.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: But frankly, today, I would say that we do not attribute the success of RI to its famous British founder and his credos, but rather, we would look to its famous Singaporean teachers, principals and vice­ principals.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: Few are more charismatic than Mr Eugene Wijeysingha.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: And I say his name because he was one of the first few people to inspire generations of Rafflesians to say that you have to give back.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: It is not enough to just do well in school for yourself; not enough to haul books at the library; not enough to ensure that your friends do well.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: The idea was always contribute back to society.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: I have friends who have graduated from other secondary schools as well.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: I have a range of friends whom I have met through National Service or work, including graduates of Maris Stella High School, Chinese High, Victoria School, St Andrews and even those of the Anglo­-Chinese School variety.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: The third and final point I want to touch on, Mr Speaker, is how when we look at the future of education, it really is a call to stare into a crystal ball but to think what are the benefits and advantages that Singaporean students would need to possess, partly because of our geography, partly because of the languages that we are encouraged to speak and that we do speak as a mother tongue and what more we can do.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: As an example, 10 years ago, in 2008, Australia came up with the Melbourne Declaration for primary and secondary school education.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: And, in that Declaration, they said this: "India, China and other Asian nations are growing and their influence on the world is increasing.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: Australians need to become 'Asia literate', engaging and building strong relationships with Asia." I think they tried to do precisely that.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: Today, they suggest that they, too, maybe one day soon, should be a member of the 10-party ASEAN block so it becomes part of Southeast Asia and not just Asia.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: They speak English; they speak very good English; they can understand smatterings of the three languages beyond English that are our national languages.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: But are we doing more to ensure they understand what really makes Asia tick?

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: Because that has to start at the secondary school level.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: It is very good that we teach Cold War, current affairs.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: It is very good that we teach about early Southeast Asian history in Thailand, Indonesia and Singapore.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: But we really have to think about what we can teach these students now that prepares them for trade and investment going forward.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: Today's Motion, Mr Speaker, is dedicated to Singapore's children whom we want to be future-ready and to the teachers who have made us who we are today.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: My son Ayden is, therefore, by common definition, a child with special needs.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: The first few months of Ayden's life was probably the most challenging period in my life.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Down's Syndrome children typically have certain associated medical conditions.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: So, at the beginning, I was at Kandang Kerbau Hospital almost every other week for a slew of medical appointments.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Other parents, whose children have special needs, would probably share similar experiences.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: In addition to the worry about the children's health, there is also always that nagging fear about their future, how society would see them, whether they will be able to take care of themselves when they grow up, what will become of them when we, the parents, pass away.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: It is not uncommon to hear this – and I believe the hon Member Ms Denise Phua would have shared this – that these parents often say that they would rather live to see their child die so that they could ensure that the child's needs are met to the end.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: A quick sensing of the current environment suggests that society, whilst now more open and accepting of people with special needs, is still not completely comfortable with them.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: They also had less favourable attitudes towards those with intellectual disabilities and autism spectrum disorder.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: The Lien Foundation's Inclusive Attitudes Study conducted in 2016 echoed this finding.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I also hear stories from parents of children with special needs about how people treat their children.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: One father shared that on one occasion, a few young children were running towards his daughter.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: They probably just wanted to play, but their caregiver was heard shouting "不要去那边！她是神经病的人!”.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Several months back, I heard on the radio, a caller commenting on a discussion on inclusivity.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: The man said that his wife is a teacher and that there is a child with special needs in her class.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: His wife must have shared her challenges with him.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: He said that he was of the view that "these children" should not be put in the same class as normal children.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: They are disruptive and cause a lot of problems to the teachers and the class.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: He felt that parents of children with special needs are in denial and they want to believe that their children are normal, so they insist that their children be in mainstream schools when they actually should be taught elsewhere.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Honestly, I understood where this gentleman was coming from.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: The challenges faced by teachers in such settings are real.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I will touch on this a little later in my speech.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: But the caller's solution to the problem offended and hurt me as a parent.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: His tone and the curt manner in which he declared his views reflected how he felt about children who are different.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: They should be taught separately, kept apart from normal children.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I appreciate it may not be completely fair to postulate from his brief remarks what he thought of people with special needs in general.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: To me, though, it felt like a rejection, that children like Ayden will always be seen as a burden, that they should be put in appropriate places.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: So, what does all this have to do with the Motion today?

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: There are many different aspects of the Motion that we can debate about today but I would like to speak about inclusive education from the perspective of persons with special needs.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: The reality is, whilst Singapore has made great strides in encouraging and promoting inclusiveness within our community, we have some way to go in truly walking the talk.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Our society is still not yet able to truly view persons with disabilities as an equally valued member of the community.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: And I believe that we can review and build our education system so as to change perceptions, normalise disabilities; so that people can appreciate that persons with special needs are simply differently abled and are of no lesser value than any other member of society.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Singapore has done a lot towards building an inclusive society.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: EM1 outlined a vision where persons with disabilities are fully integrated, empowered to reach their potential and are contributing members of society.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: However, there are still gaps and areas which we can give more attention to, so as to truly embrace people with different abilities and give them the opportunity and motivation to excel.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: A pragmatist may also say that it would be unreasonable to expect the Government to put in large resources and funding to address needs of only a small percentage of people in the community.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: But I trust one can agree that enhancing inclusiveness within our education system will bring great benefit to Singapore as a whole.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I recall a conversation I had with you, Mr Speaker, when you were then the Minister for Social and Family Development.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: You feel strongly that people with special needs have a role to play in helping build kindness and empathy in the community.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: They are conduits through which we can elevate the level of compassion amongst Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Research shows that a genuinely inclusive education system allows children to build and develop friendships that they might not have encountered otherwise, as inclusive settings encourage higher levels of interaction than segregated settings.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: What results is better outcomes for social and communication development and an early inculcation of values of inclusion.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Such early exposure benefit both children with and without special needs, where they will be better able to demonstrate greater compassion, empathy and have better understanding on how to interact with their peers and accept diversity.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: These children could develop better interpersonal skills and exhibit greater adaptability.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: These results could already be seen at Kindle Garden, a preschool by Asian Women's Welfare Association, Singapore's first inclusive preschool.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: At Kindle Garden, children with different needs and different backgrounds study together.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Learning is personalised and children are taught to embrace diversity and respect for each other.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I accept that the model is not necessarily easy to replicate, but, for now, let us focus on the results that could be achieved if we truly set out to be inclusive.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Research shows that when children with special needs are being supported to communicate with their peers, they enhance their independent communication, mastery of augmentative and alternative communication strategies and have increased speech and language development.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: If we intervene early, in schools, we give them the necessary skills and prepare them for the future, there is a greater chance that they would graduate school and join the workforce.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: If they can work well, be independent and contribute meaningfully towards the economy, less resources need to be spent on support structures or schemes when they are adults.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: In light of the above, I make the following recommendations to enhance the education landscape.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: For one, we should have an integrated education system and school setting.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: A common misunderstanding of an inclusive education is one where there is simply a presence of students with disabilities in a classroom or school setting but where micro or macro exclusion still occurs.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: If there is segregation and the children are not treated equally within the same setting, that is not truly inclusive education.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I understand that there are also lessons in Character and Citizenship Education in mainstream schools that help raise awareness of disabilities and how each person can play a part in developing an inclusive society.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Schools have also forged partnerships with Voluntary Welfare Organisations to provide opportunities for students to interact meaningfully and deepen mutual understanding.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: These are all great efforts but we need to build on them.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: So, we should have an education system where children with and without special needs learn and play within the same setting but in different pathways.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I believe that this is more accurately described as an integrated education system.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: That way, students can receive different support and assistance based on their needs but yet have the opportunity to interact meaningfully.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Currently, there are special needs students in mainstream schools.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: However, such arrangements, in some situations, have been challenging for the teachers as well as the students – those with and without special needs.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: We hear many instances where the teachers and the allied educators cannot manage the students and the class situation.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Teachers get stressed, the students in class are affected, parents chime in and express their unhappiness about the arrangements and everyone is discouraged by the efforts to be inclusive.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: So, to do this properly, we need to build the proper support structure and have sufficient resources.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: One key resource is the group of teachers who are trained to teach students with special needs.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: It appears that there is currently a shortage of such teachers.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: While there is a growing pool of allied educators specialising in learning and behavioural support and a large number of teachers trained to meet special needs in mainstream schools, teachers have been reported to be shorthanded in managing students requiring additional learning support.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: In addition, we have also seen reports in the papers about the Lien Foundation survey which alluded to a high burn-out rate of professionals working with special needs children.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: We, therefore, secondly, need to improve the profession and career pathway of special education teachers.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Currently, these teachers are hired by various social service organisations who are guided by the salary scale recommended by NCSS.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Having more educators trained in supporting special needs would better support the learning needs of our children and ensure that they can achieve their fullest potential.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: These teachers can be tapped on to support students in mainstream or SPED schools.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: In the same vein of building resources, I would make a third recommendation that we also build synergy between the education and health sectors, so as to ensure that access to the necessary assessments is enhanced.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Early identification of learning difficulties can help ensure that students who have such needs receive the necessary support as soon as possible.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: However, parents often cite long waiting lists for MOE psychologists when seeking to have their children assessed.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Lastly, I propose a review of the administration of school curriculum for both mainstream and SPED schools.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Our children are all unique, with different talents and abilities.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Often, in the school system, we are pushing them into categories or groups, which allows for a more expedient delivery of information and knowledge.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: However, this means that we may not be fully developing their strengths and addressing their weaknesses.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Support is given when their natural abilities fall short of what is required.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: But if we are really serious in allowing each child to flourish, there may be value in adjusting a curriculum according to each individual’s needs, pace of learning, as well as providing the facilities and resources required to cater to the wide spectrum of disabilities.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Can I have a copy of the amendment.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Are copies made available to Members of the House?

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Yes, I have given copies to the Clerks for distribution.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Paolo Coelho said that a child can teach an adult three things: to be happy for no reason, to always be curious and to fight tirelessly for something.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: My son teaches that to me every day.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: I am glad we are debating this Motion and I hope our children remain our most important source of inspiration.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Do I have hon Members' agreement on this?

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: The Question is, "That the words proposed to be added, be there added." Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: For the last 16 years, I have been part of the teaching and learning ecosystem in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: I am a co-founder of a purpose-driven tuition centre.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: I am a publisher of current affairs magazines sold directly to schools.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: I am also a coach and trainer of working professionals, helping them develop the social and emotional skills they need to become better architects for cultural change.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Some of my clients have included principals, vice principals, teachers and administrators.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: My interest in education began when I was 25.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: I had started an experimental tuition group with my friends because we were curious about two questions.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: We started off with 20 kids from neighbourhood JCs.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: But by the end of that same year, the group ballooned into 100 kids and we realised we should officially register as a private tuition centre.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: So, we applied to the Registry of Business (RCB) calling ourselves School of Thought and, soon after, an RCB officer called me back to tell us our name could not be approved.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: I asked him what was wrong with the name School of Thought.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: And for as long as I teach, I do not think I will forget what he said.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: His response, without any irony, was this: "What do schools have to do with thinking?

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: How do schools teach thinking?" He did not sound uneducated or unwilling, just genuinely perplexed.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: And I remember having a very surreal, one hour-long conversation with this Government officer about why schools had a lot to do with thinking, that the name was a pun and, still, he would not be moved.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Because then it's just a name, not an intention." I do not take that very odd exchange as representative of the whole-of-Government.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Also, 16 years have passed and times and attitudes have evolved since then and I am more optimistic that I would not get that response today.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Still, I do not wish to brush off his remark as an aberration.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Because his remark to me is a signpost that there could be many more individuals out there who were taught an incomplete or mistaken lesson about the purpose of education and that gap in their learning does have consequences on us all at a systemic level.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: In the last few years, I have been getting more enquiries for training from healthcare organisations.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: When we asked them why there was a surge of interest in social and emotional development from their sector, they shared with us their challenges in teaching some of their staff to see their patients as not just diseases to treat, but people to care for.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: And though the two surgeons had saved a patient in body, they had killed a young doctor in spirit.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Those kinds of stories make me reflect: when did that bureaucrat learn that schools had nothing to do with thinking?

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: When did those surgeons learn that their medical education had nothing to do with feeling?

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Did they learn it from their parents, their teachers or society?

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: And barring how great their results were in the exam hall, are we satisfied with these results of their education in real life?

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: The first 18-year-olds I taught are 34 now.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: And some of them probably work for you.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Our kids become our bureaucrats deciding what to approve or not approve.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: They become our doctors and bean-counters deciding who is worth saving and who is not worth saving.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: They become our customers and entrepreneurs deciding what money can buy and what money should never ever buy.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: They become our voters and politicians deciding who rules and who should be ruled.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: The future of our country is already being written in our classrooms.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: I do not know if that thought assures you or scares you.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: I choose to let that thought convict me to figure out how can the people continue to partner the work of our public schools so that we can all win, for our country can go only as far as our classrooms are willing and able to go.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: So, we need to work together on this.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: I will focus on three of her amendments and make my recommendations along those lines.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Her first amendment asks that we build an education system that gives each student the best possible support.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Teachers do appreciate the need to expand their work scope beyond teaching to broaden their skill sets.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: However, there is a breaking point when they start to question how much time in their job is spent on mastering their craft versus managing projects, marking, doing administrative work, running co-curricular activities (CCAs) and organising events.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Many educators actually express some guilt that they spend more time teaching and managing other people's children versus spending time on their own kids at home.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: In fact, some educators express double guilt for sending their own kids to private tuition because they have no time or energy left for their own kids after a full day of teaching.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: We must stop piling on more new initiatives and programmes onto schools because the constant cry I hear from teachers is "enough".

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: We need to do a lot less so we can do a lot more of what is significant.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Part of the reason why teachers feel so strapped for time is the number of learners we expect them to give individual attention to.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: I know MOE has argued that teacher quality matters more than class size, but the sheer volume of work to be done with such large numbers of students will constrain even the most talented teacher.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Adjunct Prof S Gopinathan at the Lee Kuan Yew School of Public Policy and former dean of National Institute of Education (NIE)'s School of Education said in an interview with The Straits Times that even the best-trained teacher will find it difficult coping with a class of 40 students in an era where we want children to be more inquisitive, explain their insights, have more applied learning.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: And those are more complex processes, compared to the direct transmissive teaching of the past.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: So, no matter how good you are as a teacher, you only have a fixed number of hours in a workday.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Even really good teachers are telling us that the only way they can cope with giving individualised attention to everyone in a large class is to sacrifice time from their after-work hours to prepare, mark, answer questions and meet up with kids.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: This is a price that many good teachers are willing to pay because of their personal convictions, but it does come at personal cost to their own mental, physical and emotional well-being.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: I see that we currently have smaller-size classes at the JCs, tertiary and university levels, but not at the primary and secondary school levels.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: I suggest that we explore our assumption that the tertiary level students need more individualised attention than younger students.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: If education is about helping learners gain in confidence and ability to manage and own their own learning process, then should not the smallest classes and the greatest availability of teacher support be with the youngest children?

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: An 18-year-old should be sufficiently independent as a learner and more capable of taking care of his own learning than a seven-year-old learner who is just beginning to "learn to learn" needs a lot more individual scaffolding and personalised attention.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: So, it does make more sense that a primary school teacher should be given a smaller class, compared to a JC teacher.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: If our education system was designed as a process of cognitive apprenticeship, then, technically, by the time you are 18, you should be able to begin teaching and learning by yourself while in teams.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: However, if our education system was not about cognitive apprenticeship and more about subject downloading, then what I have said is irrelevant.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Some of us might say that the average 18-year-old in our current system might still be exhibiting signs of great dependency on his teacher for instructions and still asking people to spot questions and compile model essays on his behalf.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: In fact, you might say some of our working adults still display similar learning habits and overdependency on authority to spoon-feed solutions.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: If so, then this is feedback that we are still not doing enough cognitive apprenticeship.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: So, to me, the class size issue is a bit linked to the intentions of our education system.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Is it for helping learners get progressively confident and independent in their thinking?

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: If so, primary school class sizes need to get much much smaller to help teachers work with their learners' high dependency.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Is it for helping learners just swallow large amounts of information?

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: If so, I can understand why huge class sizes are still tolerable because it is a bit like raising battery hens.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: You can cram a lot of them in one room because you feed them all the same thing anyway.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: But, of course, my hope and personal bias are that we go for smaller classes, because I think we should be raising more free-ranging, free-thinking independent learners because I am not sure battery cage learners will be ready to out-think and out-run the rest of the world.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: I support that request and agree with Prof Gopinathan's opinion that "more work can be done to look at the pros and cons of reducing class sizes before dismissing the idea.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Without a local knowledge base, we can't say it doesn't make a difference based on international research".

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Which brings me to the high-stakes exam issue.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: A bewildered parent explained it to me this way: "There are 10 weeks in a school term.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: The teacher typically takes Week 1 to do administration and settle the kids in.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: And then Weeks 6 to 10 are all about exam prep and taking the exam.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Where does the teacher have the time to go find out about what is happening in the world or in different industries?" When that same parent told his child's teacher that he would rather the school not focus so much on exam preparation, the teacher told him, "It’s not that I do not want to do all the interesting stuff.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: I want to, but if my students do not do well at the exams, it affects my appraisal and it affects my bonus.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: I do not have a choice." MOE has been plagued for years by public outcry about excessive levels of stress in the system.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: And while many stakeholders want the education system to change, many are still looking at other stakeholders to change first.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: So, it feels like everyone is a bit stuck in a psychological impasse.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: I have been of two minds with the issue of abolishing PSLE.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: It is hardly a silver bullet solution and abolishing it will definitely generate many new problems and fail to resolve some old ones.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: It will force many other policies to change together with it.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: However, I also see that the ground does not seem sufficiently convinced so far by the little tweaks being made to PSLE grades.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: We know this because they are not changing their behaviour in any significant way.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Mothers are still quitting their jobs to prepare their kids for PSLE.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: They are quite confident that they know their customers are not going to shift.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: The "arms race" kiasu culture seems to be eating all our strategies for breakfast.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: So, I do wonder whether abolishing PSLE could be a psychological Gordian knot that needs to be cut.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: I can understand the Government's resistance to abolishing PSLE because to take on the barrage of trouble involved, the win must be significant and something the majority of the electorate must show that it is willing to support.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Because abolishing PSLE will set off a chain reaction of very uncomfortable changes.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Without PSLE, there might be much less reason to stream in primary school or upon entering secondary school.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Primary school teachers will be challenged to up their game and compelled to design and deliver a curriculum that is no longer about preparing kids for a standardised exam.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: And MOE would have to devise a whole new way to assess the quality of teaching in primary schools without data from PSLE results.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Abolishing the PSLE also opens up the question of how then should we level the playing field for secondary schools?

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Do we want to ensure all secondary schools are funded, resourced and governed the same way by MOE?

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: If so, then we have to remove all other kinds of admissions, such as the DSA and even end the special status of some schools.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: This would be a very difficult change for some elite schools to swallow, because nobody wants to give up their elite identity.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: So, the question for us today, the Government and the people, is more about whether that steady state of greater inclusivity for all learners represents a future we think is worth suffering for.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: I do not have an answer about whether we should or should not abolish the PSLE because I recognise it takes a lot of political risk to make that change.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: So, this is all easy for me to say because I am not a politician and I am just speaking as a parent.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: This particular parent's naive hope is that we will someday dismantle the PSLE because I would rather give more time and space for our teachers to develop our children's thinking without fear of messing up a high-stakes exam.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: And this also gives us more breathing room for primary-schoolers from lower-income families to catch up.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: The second amendment Ms Rahayu Mahzam raised is about recognising the ability and talent of every student and offering developmental paths which are unique to them.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: When I talked to parents, two things were brought up.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: The first is on whether we can reimagine our report cards.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: I know we have already shifted our report cards from just listing grades and sharing more on their personal development; but I still think they do not present a rich enough picture of the unique journey of progression that every student takes.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: So, right now, the burden of assessment is placed on teachers alone.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: But what if students and parents helped to co-create the report book?

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Many preschools today actually do not use report cards and they show parents a well-curated achievement file instead.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: There is also a section in the achievement file where teachers ask parents on the spot to not only put in the parents' assessment of the achievements they have seen in their own child at home, they are even asked, very subtly, to assess what they have done for their own child.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: In my recent meeting at my daughter's preschool, I had to fill in how often we were reading to her, talking to her, showing her new places in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: They felt that, sometimes, new principals would try too hard to establish their own flavour and uproot directions set in place by the previous principal.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: This constant upheaval in direction not only prevented a strong identity and culture from forming but it broke trust with teachers and disheartened parents who believed in the previous vision.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: If more principals were allowed to commit two cycles to building culture, schools would have a stronger foundation to design those alternative development paths that are wholly unique to the school and suited to particular students' interests.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: The third amendment asks us to enable Singaporeans to improve our lives and pay special attention to the kids from vulnerable families.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: In this, I want to raise our attention to an especially vulnerable niche group of kids: those who grow up under the care of single migrant mothers.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: This is a group that was highlighted to me by ReadAble, which is a wonderful ground-up movement of young professionals who partner lower-income families to close the literacy gap.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: For the last four years, they have been running literacy classes in Jalan Kukoh, not just for the kids but for their mothers as well.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: These kids are three to 14 years old.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: They do not speak English as a first language at home.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Many still cannot name all the letters of the alphabet.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: This means, without any early intervention, many of the kids would have begun Primary 1 with no or little reading skills.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: This puts them way behind the starting line.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Research very clearly shows that early intervention in the lives of children from low socio-economic status (SES) households would reduce the learning gap significantly in the following years of their lives.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: In fact, some of the kids who attend their preschool class currently read better than children who joined them at primary school-age.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: So, there is a trickle-down effect as well.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: As the kids grow in confidence, they started to influence their siblings to read.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: I hope the Government can partner community groups to intervene as early as possible in the literacy gap.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: For instance, can the National Library place a personalised mini-library in every low-income household with a child that requests to have one?

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Every parent in this room also knows there is a huge difference when children grow up in a literacy-rich environment.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: That is why we buy books for our kids though we also have access to public libraries.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: So, we allow these kids to initiate the request for their own mini-library and own their own customised cargo of books.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: They might be far more likely to see books as part of their life.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: If the Media Development Authority can consider working with these successful ground-up literacy movements to co-create a solution using media or technology that could help sustain their impact, that would be great because kids need plenty of repetition and audio-visual recordings of these books for them to play back at their own time might prove really helpful.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Second, can the Government provide better support in housing, education and employment for migrant mothers who are struggling to improve the lives of their Singaporean children?

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: A stable home environment and literacy-related support for these parents will help the child's educational progress and more deliberate and pre-emptive outreach from the Government to help these migrant mothers care for their Singaporean child in the short run could stave off far more expensive problems in the long run.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Community groups like ReadAble, working directly with such migrant mothers, hope for much greater public dialogue on how they can partner the state to help more migrant mothers and their Singaporean children progress in the education aspect.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: There is, in fact, a school in Singapore that manifests so many of the things I talked about in this speech.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Character Education there already makes up 50% of its first two years of curriculum and is a major part of the way they assess student development.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: The kids there are focused on discovering their values and what work they would like to do and not just mug before an exam.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: By the end of their programme, they would have all gone for an eight-week industry attachment.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: And, yes, they have achievement records, not report cards, and their kids are so proud to show them to their parents.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: And, yes, there are protected times there for educators to just reflect and learn.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: And, yes, this is a school that gives support to its neighbourhood community and receives a lot of support back from its community.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Northlight is a school that makes me damn proud to be Singaporean.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Honestly, I would gladly send my own child there.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: I have five key reasons for making this call: one, we need to urgently respond to the rapid rise in global changes and disruptions; two, we need to broaden the definition of education; three, we cannot afford to ignore the elephants in the current education system; four, no one knows it all; and five, no one can do it all.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Reason one: response to the rapid rise in global changes and disruptions.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: The world's largest movie supplier owns no cinemas – that is Netflix.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: One of the world's largest accommodation providers owns no physical real estate – that is Airbnb.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Even the beggars in some countries, such as China, are tapping on technology to collect monies – cashless.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: As former Google Senior Vice President Rosenberg puts it, "… the world is changing so fast across every industry and endeavour, that it is a given that the role for which you are hiring is going to change." No one knows for certain what the jobs of the future will be, but we know that progressive employers are looking for candidates who have high-learning agility, candidates who learn on their own, candidates who are comfortable in moving out of comfort zones.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: The MOE team had been working hard to update Singapore's education system.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Over the years, we have heard of separate reviews in early childhood, special schools, primary schools, secondary schools, Institutes of Technical Education, polytechnics, universities and in the adult learning space as well.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Reason two: our need to broaden the definition of education.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Many of our education initiatives were made with the purpose of ensuring that as many Singaporeans as possible can be economically deployed.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Nothing wrong with that; after all, a vibrant economy and full employment pay the bills and fund the public services, including helping our poor.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: But the future of Singapore is more than just the future state of its economy and its workforce.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: A good education must surely lead to a good life, a better life for the people; a better life that is more than holding down a good job and attaining financial wellness.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: It should not have to take a World Health Organization (WHO) study to inform us that a better life must also include physical wellness, socio-emotional wellness, passion for learning and the important component of service to others.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: To what extent has our existing education system led us to a better life?

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Have the schooled amongst us learnt and adopted healthy lifestyles after we leave school?

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Have we learnt to build strong personal relationships?

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Have we, young and older, developed a love for learning and taken responsibility for our own learning?

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Have we regularly given time and efforts for people and causes beyond ourselves?

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: What kind of education, for what kind of society?

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Intellects like John Abbott from the 21st Century Learning Initiative, lamented on what he felt was the sad state of the British education system.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: In his writing, "Battling for the Soul of Education", John Abott asked the pertinent question of "What kind of education for what kind of world?".

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: He issued a clarion call for an education to prepare the young "for the kind of adult life which society values and which society wishes to perpetuate." He said, "Develop the young to be "thinkers able to take responsibility for their own actions, and willing to accept responsibility for working for the common good.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Re-imagine society first; and then the education system." Hence, an education masterplan for the future must convey and communicate the definition of a good education that reflects the kind of society we want.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Next, Sir, I want to talk about the elephants in the room: the obvious difficulties in our system that people often do not wish to talk about.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: The elevation of one's place in life as an outcome of one's better endowed and ambitious parents; as a result of one's academic abilities; as a result of other abilities that are not due to class privilege – they are all outcomes of Singapore's success story. "Parentocracy", meritocracy and the resulting inequalities are all developments that have come under criticism in recent times.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: The Straits Times' Chua Mui Hoong pointed out in her book, "Singapore Disrupted" that "Singapore's academic-based system of meritocracy needs to evolve." Already, she said, "Many critics have pointed to the limits of Singapore's competitive examination-based academic meritocracy, which has bred a generation of hyper-competitive students who try to top examinations… to secure a place in that cherished school or to win that prestigious scholarship", she said.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: The findings of a recent Mediacorp Channel 8 Education Survey of 1,200 respondents are cause for concern.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: It was reported that more children are enrolling in more tuition as they rise through the school levels, spending even longer hours in tuition at the secondary level.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Tuition is no longer only about providing support to those who are performing badly.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: It is a way to, as they say, "hack the examinations".

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: But there is an underlying layer of fear in our system of high-stakes examinations that is killing us softly: the fear of failing; the fear of not doing well enough; the fear of not being able to get into the next school of our choice; the fear of what it looks on our resume; and even the fear of what else we should chase if we are not chasing these marks.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Joy and this brand of unhealthy fear should not co-exist.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Fear strips away the joy of learning; fear distracts us from the real "why" of learning.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: We are the victims of our own success.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: It is up to us, the people of Singapore, to craft a new narrative.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: We cannot continue to tweak the edges of the current education system.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: More of us have to stand up to seek and articulate a more compelling, a more hopeful vision versus this relatively uninspiring and utilitarian state of learning.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: We need to not just think out of the box; we may need to get rid of the box to confront some of these elephants in the room.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: No one, nobody, not even MOE, has the monopoly of wisdom and perspective to get it right.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: We have to unpack them so that we can move ahead with clarity and courage.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Like me, I am sure many of you have lost count of how many new topics MOE has been asked to add to its curriculum.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Today, you will hear from us, parliamentarians a host of what should be added: digital skills, life skills, financial literacy, art and music, sports, Asian literacy and, of course, not forgetting new economy literacy topics like coding, computational thinking, data analytics and so forth.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Minister Chan Chun Sing himself joined the chorus last week when he implored the Public Service to acquire four sets of new skills: digital skills, design thinking skills, systems skills and ability to collaborate across society.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: The World Economic Forum listed 10 skills to survive what is now called the Fourth Industrial Revolution and named complex problem solving, critical thinking, creativity and cognitive flexibility, amongst them.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Experts visualise a picture of more personalised learning driven by a more individual self-paced curriculum; lesser physical campuses, project and problem-based learnings; teachers as guides, curators of content and learning designers; and social and emotional skills.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Everyone – from babies to youths to working adults to seniors; and not forgetting those of us who learn differently and those of us who are at risk of being left behind; the disadvantaged and persons with special needs.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Reason five: no one can do it all.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Families with younger children must take our place and decide that enough is enough.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: We will not live in fear; we will not succumb to the excesses of a tuition nation.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Families must not simply outsource the raising of our children, building of character and life skills in their children to domestic helpers, schools and vendors.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Educators in schools must do their part to be relevant and updated.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: They must themselves be self-driven learners and become better designers of learning experiences; curators of content; and coaches to instil life skills, such as problem-solving, teamwork and social resilience, in partnership with caregivers and students themselves.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: The community must provide opportunities and training to ensure purposeful and fruitful internships and service learning assignments.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Adult learners need to rise to the challenge of being personally responsible for our own learning, not just dependent on the SkillsFuture Credit or the courses that have been created for us.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: The Government must be the systems integrator to harness the energies of all key stakeholders; to apply design and systems thinking skills to facilitate the crafting of an integrated and dynamic education masterplan.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: There are and there will be no single brilliant strategist; and no magic silver bullet to craft an education for the future.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: We must all come together and craft and support an education masterplan that is uniquely Singapore.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: But I fear this is one of the key factors why we often resort to just tweaking the system, instead of making bolder moves – for fear of changing a system that earned us so much prestige.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: But let us learn something from the World Cup series that is going on now.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: I am speaking about the Motion today on imagining Education for Our Future, I think we should examine present trends, which will help us forecast possible future scenarios, should the situation remain the same.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: So, what do we see today that can impact on our future?

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: The above troubling signs might seem pessimistic, but, as my favourite writer 木心（Mu Xin) says: "悲观是一种远见".

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: In identifying possible negative outcomes, we can then work harder collectively to come up with new ways of addressing these crises before they become reality.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: I say "collectively" because I believe it is essential for us to break away from the sense of alienation many of us feel when faced with these challenges.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: To do that, we must better understand the complexities of these disruptions, so that we can present better suggestions to tackle them.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: To better understand the future that young people wish to see, recently, I asked a group of youths about their hopes, dreams and concerns.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Amongst the responses included: a call for transparency, that truths should not be distorted just so that some can achieve their personal goals; a plea for kindness to others, especially those who are different from us; and an exhortation for everyone to collaborate and work together, rather than pursue self-serving gains; and one particularly poignant call by this young lady who said, she hopes, we, as human beings, do not lose our faith in humanity.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: All these hopes, shared by youths, are heartening because they point to a few key points: open-heartedness, teamwork, deep listening and engagement, all of which are essential for true, constructive discourse.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Yet, in recent times, when there is disagreement, people resort to one of two modes: either to "agree to disagree" and just leave it at that; or to "disagree" vehemently, engage in keyboard warrior tactics on the Internet, or wage a litany of complaints on other channels.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: There is no empathy or desire to listen.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: But what is disconcerting is that that was a simplistic misreading of an artistic work.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Is this the sort of discourse we want for our future, a reactionary one that seeks to ban works, complain, call out, label and shame without dialogue?

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Why does one group so quickly jump to impose its moral value on others?

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Why should the louder voice always be the one abided to, before all sides tell their story and come to a point of agreement with negotiation and mediation?

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Is it that the complainant's version of truth is the singular one everyone else must accept?

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: The world does not comprise only one simplistic moral or ethical view.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Just like how we look at one object by not only observing the parts that are lit, but also those defined by shadows, so it is that the world comprises different shades, contexts and perspectives.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: I bring this up because discourse is something fundamental and integral in education, specifically in the study of the humanities.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Through Literature, History, Geography and the Arts, we develop a keen sensibility for nuances, differences and complexities.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Take, for instance, the Dream of the Red Chamber, which, when studied from a humanistic approach, is not just a literature text to be examined.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Rather, it is a very nuanced study of humankind, of society, of politics, of culture and art.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: We discover that being human, through that book, means having to deal with the different aspects of living: social, political, emotional, psychological, spiritual, physical, carnal and meta-physical.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Yes, the Dream of Red Chamber does talk about carnal desires.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: We learn that power of empathy, by seeking to understand and deeply appreciate how each of these characters are like and, of course, including their shadows.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Because we do not want a future society without empathy.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Education plays such a crucial role here, because our young ones should be given the opportunity to explore in schoo,l under the guidance of teachers, so that they learn at a tender age about the complexities of humanity.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Without this, we will likely have a generation of people lacking in empathy, believing only in one's value and unable to comprehend or accept vulnerability in human existence.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: In fact, even in the study of science, technology, mathematics, the focus is not merely on the discovery of theorems, theories and inventing things.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Rather, great scientists and inventors view nature with awe and are constantly searching for humanity's relationship with nature, to understand rather than to alter it.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: This is because they are acutely aware that the search for truth is a quest in humility.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: And in acknowledging our imperfection and ignorance, we open our hearts and minds to learn and improve.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: As Lessing, the philosopher, put it succinctly: it is not the truth that a man possesses, or believes that he possesses, but the earnest effort which he puts forward to reach for truth which constitutes the worth of a man.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: So, where would be the best place for such complex studies of the humanities happen?

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Naturally, it is in our educational institutions, which provide a safe space where our young people can grapple with these conundrums in life, ponder deeply about differences, and come to a better understanding of and empathy for others.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: This is also how educators help develop critical thinking in the young.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: In Singapore, we have been emphasising the importance of critical thinking.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: But critical thinking is not just about differentiating what is good or bad, or what works or not.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: In teaching critical thinking, a lot of emphasis has been placed on the methodology of problem-solving.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: That is to say, one learns to analyse the problem, then suggest solutions, before evaluating its results.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: There is also an emphasis on dialogic learning.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Allow me to quote Paulo Freire, the pedagogue who advocated Problem Posing approach, dialogic learning and critical pedagogy.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: To him, dialogue "cannot exist without the profound love for the world", and Problems-posing Education "affirms men and women as being in the process of becoming".

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: So, a good critical thinker is someone who has a curiosity in how human beings think, act and feel.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: This desire to understand another person’s perspective, objectives, fears and hope is the first step towards critical thinking and then towards empathy.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: The study of humanities will go a long way in developing our critical thinking skills.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: It should and must be an integral part of our pedagogical approach towards knowledge acquisition and the overall formation of our youths.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: I spoke earlier about curiosity being a building block of critical thinking.
