speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: I believe that people – young and old alike – are inherently curious folks.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: We want to know how things work, why policies are made, when something will affect us and how extensive that will be.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Yet, as the saying goes, many may buy into the notion that "curiosity kills the cat".

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Asking too many questions is sometimes seen as diverting energies in something that is irrelevant; it sidetracks from the task orientation.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: In a world that seeks efficiency, maximised profit and maximum satisfaction, it is easy to take the beaten and proven path, but, by doing so, we have sacrificed our natural instinct for curiosity as well.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: I remember how my Mathematics professor in NUS, Prof Lee Peng Yee, proved theorems during lectures.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: He certainly knew all the right steps to do so, but, interestingly, he would deliberately permit himself to take detours, try alternatives, until he met with an obstacle.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Was he wasting his students' time as he meandered and hit roadblocks?

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: In fact, his trajectory was illuminating, because as he traced his steps back, he talked about why this path did not work and how we could perhaps try another path instead.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: His deep curiosity was infectious and I remember it fondly until now.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Curiosity is about getting lost, but allowing oneself to do so without fear.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Any inventor or artist will tell you the same thing: that the fun part of creation is when you are trying to find your way around, when you are experimenting and discovering the world in the process.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: There should be no fear in that, but, rather, we should become accustomed to the promise that it brings with it.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Once again, the question is: where is the best and safest space to allow young people to be lost and explore?

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: They are well-equipped to guide young people, young explorers and creators in life, as they find their own individual paths.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Through these detours, they can discover curvatures and gradients instead of a straightforward movement from Point A to B.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: They can explore shapes and shades and become more three-dimensional in their outlook.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: I do not know how many teachers can do as Prof Lee did in my Mathematics classes.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: I do not know how many young people get to benefit from that curiosity, so that they learn what does not work as much as what can.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: In today's competitive, results-oriented world, we tussle to be Number One all the time.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: This narrative has also permeated our education system and has become part of our cultural DNA.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: We may laugh about how Singaporeans are kiasu and kiasi, but, in accepting these traits with humour, we are also legitimising these self-serving attitudes and behaviour; we have normalised this race for instant gratification, for accolades, when we are winners and not second best.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: So, to ensure results, we instil discipline and rigour.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: We tell our young people, yes, it is good for you to try new things, but make sure you get those grades or you will fall behind in life.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: We remind them that life is a competition, fulfilment is to be the best.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: But is competition the best way that we can be?

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Should we create a race to the last for 5.6 million individuals, so that some privileged ones amongst us, or some able-bodied amongst us, can be the best?

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Can our education system reflect an ideal of how we want our society to be, like what fellow Member, Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng, has just said?

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: In my opinion, the schools are places where we can learn such life skills, that there is much merit in collaboration.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: A proliferation of competition can lead to a cancerous situation.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: In removing competitive elements from our education system, schools can become more inclusive and equitable and young people can discover the full potential of their innate curiosity.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Humanities and the cultivation of curiosity is not only reserved for the academically inclined.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Unlike the situation during my time in school, you no longer need to be more proficient in language and writing to be studying literature or the arts.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Rather, curiosity is a leveller – it is present whether you are academically inclined or otherwise and it should continue to be nurtured, regardless of how smart, or privileged you are.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: But I can imagine what a rebuttal to this might be: do we have time to be curious?

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: How do we make time for quality learning through discovery and having deep discussions on the humanities?

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: A parent of a young boy once told me that her kid had initially enjoyed preschool, which was full of play and discovery.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: But the moment he went to kindergarten, the pressure of academic pursuit reared its ugly head.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: By the time he was in Primary 3, when the PSLE loomed ominously ahead in the coming years, the honeymoon period was over.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: She noticed that her son had lost his sense of curiosity.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: I am aware that this question has been mooted before, but I believe it is important for us to ponder more deeply about it even now.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: If young students have to prepare for a major examination after an initial six years of study, does it impede their ability to learn deeply, discover and investigate?

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: I think we need to fundamentally agree on what is important in the education of our young people.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: If so, can we rethink the current system to make time for these aspects, rather than rush them through national examinations that determine their paths at so tender an age?

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: I have heard sharings of young people talking about how PSLE is such a scary thing.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Children who studied so hard yet could not get the results he wanted and became angry and smashed a chair.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: I am a product of such kind of education.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: The competition, the exam, the pressure that comes with shame and fear.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: And I still have nightmares of not completing my examination.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: It was only in theatre that I found the meaning of collaboration.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: When we are working in productions, when we use the best of our abilities to make the most meaningful work.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Theatre-making provides a different model of learning: working with each other's strengths, respecting each other's differences, incorporating different opinions for the sake of trying to present a complex world of existence.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: The Scandinavian system has provided certain possibilities for us to look at.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Of course, I am not saying that we simply emulate their system.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Naturally, for any change, there is a need for plenty of political will and the Government and people must commit to such a change.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: But as a start, I think it is important to begin discussing this process of change, so that we can chart a roadmap forward, as well as addressing parents' anxiety over the issue.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: I would not talk about classroom sizes because my colleague, Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin, has talked about it.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: But I want to talk about assessment again, which I think is an important aspect of learning.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Many of us are aware of diagnostic assessment, where assessment is used to diagnose students' needs, so that the learning process can be improved to help them acquire knowledge better.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: In short, diagnostic assessment is less about KPIs, more about taking the interest of each individual child at heart.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: It means education to harness his or her skills, to address his or her needs and to encourage and groom each child's unique strengths.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: It changes the relationship between teachers and parents, between teachers and students, and amongst students themselves.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: It becomes an approach that is not about competition and not about fighting to be the best, but more about discovery, collaboration and being the best together, rather than alone.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: I will talk about the educators who are instrumental in shaping our young people.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: I have worked with teachers for many years and we have heard about how much they have done and a lot of event-organising they have done.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: In fact, there is a joke that goes around that if they want a second career, they can consider being event-organisers.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: I know from personal encounter that most teachers are incredibly passionate about teaching and draw their greatest pleasure from daily interactions with students.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: However, with increasing demands on how lessons should be taught – for instance, new pedagogical approaches, such as inquiry-based learning, or "Teach Less, Learn More" model – teachers who are products of our previous education system have found it challenging to move into these methods.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: It is not for the lack of trying or an unwillingness to try, but that they need more time to adapt and experiment.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: I know intimately the pressures of parenting and I am familiar with the worries any parent has about the well-being and performance of our kids in schools.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Parents are equally responsible in the education of our children.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Have we also passed on that role of education fully to teachers, rather than undertake part of it ourselves?

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: So, here is my plea to parents like myself.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: A teacher has to take care of more than one class of students.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Your child's teacher has more wards than just your kid.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Mr Kok, you have half a minute left.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: We hope that parents will also take heed.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This is a phrase we are very familiar with by now.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Perhaps soon, we will also have to say, "every early childhood development centre (ECDC) is a good early childhood development centre".

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Parents are now not just worried about which primary school their child goes to but also which ECDC their child goes to.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The rat race has now begun way before our primary schools.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We now have kindergarten assessment books, tuition for preschool children and even homework for our nursery kids.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I have to be honest to say that this worries me.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My wife and I found ourselves in this rat race as we searched for an ECDC to send our daughter Ella to.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The reality is that there is a wide variety of ECDCs.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We tried a few, visiting them, letting Ella try it out for a day to see if she liked it and I joined her during these trials.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I sat there in some of the ECDCs and I saw first-hand how much things have changed.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: As Mdm Siti Zubaidah said in a news article, "In the past, it was all play and just learning the ABCs in kindergarten.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: But now, by K1, you need to learn how to count and read, to be on a par with everyone else”.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In a post by ex-MOE policy officer, Yann Wong, in June this year, he also mentioned about how performance anxiety, shame and a need for validation through grades are problems that plague our students and our education system.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The early childhood years should really be about play.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: As O Fred Donaldson had said, “Children learn as they play.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Most importantly, in play, children learn how to learn.” The early years are the most formative in a child’s development, character and future.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Scientific research tells us that children have objective developmental stages.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Below the age of seven, especially, they need large amounts of time for free play.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This develops personal and social awareness, gross and fine motor skills, and a foundation for learning.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It is more important to directly encounter the things in the world that words and numbers describe, than to recite those words and numbers in an academic way.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Earlier is not better when it comes to academic learning as well.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: A New Zealand study looked at children who read at five versus those who read at seven.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: They had no difference in reading outcomes at age 15.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In the German system, young children focus on social and personal awareness, only learning to read and write at age seven.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This nation is also a major engineering and economic powerhouse of the world.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: An education for our future needs to look at solutions that are both holistic and inclusive for our children, parents and educators.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: First, we can strengthen and lead the move to de-emphasise academic content for early childhood education.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The present emphasis on academics means that children play less and they are also outdoors less.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Studies again in this area show that a lack of play will increase the odds of depression, anxiety and other disorders.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We also need to help shift the current tuition mindset for preschool children.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: As Dr Nirmala Karuppiah, an early childhood and special education lecturer at the National Institute of Education, stated in a news article, "As tuition is about sitting at a table doing pencil and paper activities as well as rote learning and acquiring academic skills, it could actually cause more harm than good for some children.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: For example, it goes against the way young children grow, develop and learn, which is through play and interacting with real objects, people and events in their environment." Following on this point is, second, we need to promote more play and exploration in preschools and also lower primary schools.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In the early years, children learn mainly through active exploration of the environment.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In the words of Albert Einstein, "Play is the highest form of research." In fact, our current "Nurturing Early Learners" curriculum already recognises that children are naturally curious and does outline a framework that encourages learning through play.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: However, I am not sure whether this is followed by all ECDCs.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: From what I have seen and what other parents have shared online and with me, play is not a strong focus in some of the ECDCs.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We also need to look into how we can provide our early childhood educators with enough time and flexibility to allow for creative exploration and play.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Third, we need to put care even more at the forefront to cater to the individual needs of each child.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The need for young children to form responsive relationships cannot be overstated.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Our policies and early learning framework should support the ability of educators and caregivers to be sensitive and responsive to a young children’s needs.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: To support caregivers and educators, it is vital that student-to-teacher ratio remains small so that each child receives the attention he or she needs.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: To prevent disruptive relationships between caregivers and children in their care, it is also important to reduce the rate of turnover in these positions.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Attractive salaries, incentives and supervision should be put in place for educators of young children.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: When children feel cared for in a stable and supportive relationship, stress naturally goes away and learning takes care of itself.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In fact, shifting our priority to care over academic outcomes is key in helping children thrive and reach their full potential.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Fourth, the future of our education requires us to cater to the emotional health of students more comprehensively.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I am heartened to see that schools remain vigilant in preventing further suicides in children.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We want children to thrive, not simply survive.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Approximately half the parents interviewed were concerned that the educational system did not support students to develop these qualities.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: While there are existing frameworks on Southampton Emotional Literacy Scales (SELS), some surveys show that more can be done, and should be done, to meet the emotional needs of students.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Other studies likewise indicate that feeling socially connected as a child is more strongly associated with happiness in adulthood than academic achievement is.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Lastly, I propose a need to review the performance-based ranking for teachers.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It provides a competency-based performance management system which serves to appraise teachers' efforts for the year.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The EPMS Teaching Competency Model, among other indicators, assesses a teacher's ability to "cultivate knowledge".

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In an interview on incentives in education, American psychologist Barry Schwartz said, "If you start giving teachers bonuses if their students exceed some scores on these standardised tests, teachers will find a way to teach to the test.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Test scores will go up, but education will not." Teachers join teaching to make a difference to the lives of our youths.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Yet, the reality of the pressure from competition created by our own performance-based ranking and reward system can skew teachers’ choices.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We want teachers who teach for the love of teaching, not teachers who teach for tests.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Perhaps, there should also be a de-emphasis of ranking and rewarding of teachers based on ranking.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Ranking teachers pits them against each other and may incentivise some teachers to do what is visible or measurable, like teach to teach, to the test.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Educators are pitted against each other, which could also reduce the incentive for some to share resources and ideas, or to work together.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: And this, definitely, cannot be the case for our preschool children.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In the words of Fred Rogers, "Play is often talked about as if it were a serious relief from serious learning.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Play is really the work of childhood." Sir, I support the Motion.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: (In Malay):  : Hon Mr Speaker, I agree and acknowledge that we have a world-class education system, which, at times, is the envy of other countries.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: Our nation has developed for over five decades, during which time our education system has played an important role in our success.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: The Malay community, in general, has achieved success in many fields.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: We can see many young Malays now who are highly educated and attained their own successes.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: The focus on getting the right education is something that, undeniably, leads to all these successes.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: However, there are those within our community who are not as fortunate.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: As we strive and progress towards building an inclusive society, where no one should be left behind, I think that there is more that we can do for our students.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: We must be bold in our actions, beyond merely giving lip service about levelling the playing field for everyone.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: We must make hard decisions and take bold actions, no matter how difficult it might be, in order to create a level playing field.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: We must strive to mitigate the different obstacles faced by our children in order to help them succeed and achieve their dreams and aspirations.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: We must go beyond merely using buzzwords like "future-ready" or "broad-based education".

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: These words may sound good, but are they well-understood or seen as reality by the man-in-the-street?

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: Just as we work towards building a society with a big heart, our education system has to develop its strategies with a heart.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: This kind of education strategy needs to be holistic in nature, which focuses on the development of each individual, in order to explore the potential and grow the capabilities of each child, so as to help them achieve their dreams and aspirations.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: Let us take this step together and embolden ourselves to achieve this objective, so as to ensure a successful life for our future generations.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: The strategies that we create must take into account the abilities and shortcomings of each individual and transform it into opportunities to grow and thrive.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: In our eagerness to do so, we must ensure that it does not limit their opportunities.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: It requires all stakeholders – the Government, schools, teachers, students and parents – to join hands and work together.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: But I am certain that this is a goal that is shared by everyone.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: With this common goal, we hope that we can take our first step towards achieving national integration, where everyone moves forward together as one nation, with no one left behind, and each individual, whether children or adults, can thrive on their own abilities without being limited by the system.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: Let us take this bold step together for the sake of our future generations.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: (In English): Mr Speaker, I shall now deliver my speech in English.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: Education is an often-discussed topic that I foresee will continue to be hotly debated in the years to come.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: This is certainly to be expected as education has such a tremendous impact on our future generations and the state of our economy.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: Education also plays a major role in the social mobility of our citizens.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: We have repeatedly told our students, "Go, go and get a good education, and you will have a better future".

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: And that is true, for the most part.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: But what if one's starting point affects one's ability to have a good education?

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: What if one's circumstances present him or her with challenges and difficulties which hinder him or her in getting a good education?

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: As an illustration, a child from a low-income family, in most cases, starts out at a disadvantage.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: Despite the assistance that they receive or that is made available to them, there is a high chance that their performance in school may still be affected by other factors, such as their living conditions, the strength of the family unit and others.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: These are the very real circumstances that our students are going through and something needs to be done to help them.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: As Singapore progresses and develops further, we must ensure that every individual is sufficiently equipped to face the uncertain future.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: Let us make our education system a platform for all, to enable them to rise up in meeting with the new challenges.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: As we work towards an inclusive society where no one is left behind, I think there is still much that can be done for our students and it has to go beyond lip service about levelling the playing field.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: It has to go beyond catchphrases like "future-ready" or "broad-based education".

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: But is this well-understood by the average person?

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: Can the common man truly see the reality?

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: It is about developing strategies that consider the child holistically and as an individual who is unique.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: We should consider to develop strategies that make pathways available to them that are truly meaningful in helping them to achieve their aspiration and dream and the true meaning of success.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: We should be bold enough to take the step forward to consider multiple education systems and strategies with different approaches to serve the varying individual needs, a holistic system where every dream and aspiration is met.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: And I am convinced we have the ability and maturity to do this.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: Strategies have to take into account the child's abilities and shortcomings and turn these into opportunities to grow and thrive.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: However, we must be careful that, in our pursuit, we do not limit opportunities for them.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: Admittedly, this is a difficult task and it is one that requires all stakeholders to work together – the Government, schools, teachers, educators, students and parents.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: But I am certain that this is a goal that is shared by everyone and it is within this shared goal that we can hope to take our first step forward in achieving national integration, where everyone moves forward together as one, with no one left behind and everyone thrives, based on their abilities without being limited by the system.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: Let us take this bold step together for the sake of our future generation.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: As we talk about the importance of developing skills rather than chasing for degrees, how have we seen the decision of parents and students change?

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: We need to look at why this is so.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: Could there be a lack of understanding of what it means to be future-ready?

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: If so, then, clearly, outreach and education efforts need to be stepped up.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: Yet, if we ask parents, many may not see this as being true.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: Anecdotally, I have heard parents of lower primary students lamenting about how tough school work is for their children these days.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: How can the abstract concept of modelling be effectively and comprehensively explained to an eight-year-old child who is only two years into the primary school system?

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: Is our education system, in its pursuit to be competitive, inadvertently taking away the joy of learning?

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: How are our students supposed to spend time to explore and discover their love for Mathematics, if they are inundated with planning out models for problem sums today?

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: Shall we not guide our students to discover what they do not know and assist them to explore alternatives, rather than providing concepts and solutions?

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: I believe the ability to discover, explore and rediscover will have a more far-reaching effect in the long run.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: Our goal to become a resilient nation should embark on a "discover and explore" education system, continually.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: Ideally, education should be about allowing our children to explore the different subjects at their own pace and discover what interests them.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: Admittedly, it would not be easy to achieve.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: But challenges and obstacles have never stopped us as a nation, so why let them stop us now?

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: A child who learns because he wants to will learn and retain much more than one who feels forced to do so simply because it will count towards his final grade.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: My concern is that the chase for grades will make our children lose sight of what is important – that it is truly a joy to learn new things.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: My concern is that the preoccupation with doing well and being the best will derail them from the essence of learning, which is to discover new things that interest them, that will fuel their curiosity and desire to explore and learn even more.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: It is my hope that the Government and policymakers will approach education strategies with a heart, especially in considering the different circumstances our children are in and how we can help them overcome any challenges or barriers.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: It is also my hope that these strategies will also help our children to explore and rediscover the joy of learning.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: Only when we do these can we truly prepare our children for the future and, at the same time, take our first step towards achieving national integration, where everyone moves forward together as one, with no one left behind.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: It is through education that we progress and morph from one stage to the next.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: Be it in culture, economics, engineering or others, education will continue to be the bridge for now and into the future, enabling us to be socially mobile.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: However, like the generations before us, our future will always be challenged with uncertainties as the external environment is dynamically changing.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: I am certain that our ability to explore and discover will enable us to circumvent these uncertainties and lead us to the right survival strategies.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: Let us be bold, bold enough to explore new ideas to ensure that our education system brings out the best in each and every one of us.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: With that, Mr Speaker, without reservation and, wholeheartedly, I support the Motion.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Leveraging on our human capital has allowed us to thrive and punch far above our weight on the global stage and is a testament to our efforts to develop, attract and retain human capital.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: A key ingredient to sustaining Singapore's talent competitiveness and enhancing our human capital is a robust ecosystem that supports our human capital development and education is a critical aspect of that system.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Indeed, it is this belief in the importance of education that led me to begin my career as an educator in 2001 and it is this belief that motivates me to continue in my career as an educator today.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Over the years, Singapore has made changes to its education system to ensure that it continues to be relevant.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: With education being the key to developing people to their full potential, we need to continue to be innovative and visionary in our approach and ensure that we have an education system that not only develops our people to their full potential, but also one that helps them meet the challenges of the 21st century.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: By an "I"-graduate, I mean the horizontal top of the "I" will refer to a spread of different technical skills and knowledge, one of which will then go deep to form the vertical part of the "I" and then, the bottom horizontal bar of the "I" will refer to a variety of life skills and other skills that will actually anchor the individual in the journey through life.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The call for creating "I"-shape graduates has far more relevance today than before, especially in this age of disruption.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Across the globe, we have seen disruptions happening not only in businesses, but also in how we work, play and organise our lives.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: As the operating landscape of our lives becomes more complex, it is now more important than ever to ensure that our youths and young adults possess a diverse set of skills that allow them to traverse and navigate this increasingly pluralistic world.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Ellen Galinsky, the co-founder of Family and Work Life Institute in the USA, advocated that we need to possess seven life skills that allow us to grow and learn throughout our lives.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This self-directed and engaged learning would, indeed, be an indication of the "love for learning" concept that is mentioned in the Motion today.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In an increasingly complex world where simple linear relationships are giving way to multi-directional ones, our youths need to see both the wood and the trees.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This would require them to be perceptive and have the intuitive ability to make connections between seemingly unconnected events and make sense of them.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I would also like to take some time to talk about the issue of tuition and education, Mr Speaker.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This has been mentioned by Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan in his opening speech; by my colleague Mr Louis Ng and a few other colleagues.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I think there is a tendency to regard tuition as the scourge of our education system.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I think the issue here is perhaps one that I feel strongly about and, that is, for parents to understand how tuition fits into the education of their children.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I know a lady who lives in my constituency and we see her quite often at grassroots events.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I used to see her with her child.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: And increasingly, on the weekends, her child would be with her less and less.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: And I actually asked her one day, "Where is your child?" she said, "Oh, he is having tuition".

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The next week, I saw her again and I asked, "Where is your child?" She said, "He is having tuition." And one day, I asked her, I said, "Madam, you don't mind if I ask you, why is it your child seems to be going for a lot of tuition on the weekends?

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Shouldn't he be here with you having some fun?" She said, "What to do?

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: If I don't send him for tuition, he is never going to do his work." And I think this comment by this lady had me reflecting because, essentially, what she was hoping to do was that by sending her child for tuition, that will eventually "cure" him, as it were, of the concern that he was lazy and not wanting to do his work.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I think that is reflective of how parents then would view tuition in the context of their children's education.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: By all means, if your child needs tuition, I think we should be supportive of families who are needy, help them get the tuition.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: And if people can afford tuition, then get tuition for your children if they need to improve and if they are struggling with their subjects.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: But I would hope parents would also encourage their children to take ownership of their learning, to be these self-directed learners that we are talking about, rather than regard tuition as a way of ensuring that children do their work.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The danger of this, Mr Speaker and Members of the House, is that we will end up with a society, one day, whereby when the tuition finally stops, then what do you do?

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: What do you do when there is no one left to tell you how to do your work?

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: When there is no one left to tell you what assignments you should do?

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: When there is no one left to tell you which 10-year series you should practise?

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Because you cannot have tuition throughout your entire life.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Or maybe you can and that is why people have life coaches, psychologists and psychiatrists.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Moving on then to my next topic, which is: an exam-based academic achievement versus a skills-based academic achievement.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I think one way of ensuring that we focus more on life skills is to explore how we can shift from an exam-based academic system to a more coursework-based or skills-based academic one.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I spent 16 years in the polytechnic as an educator and I have seen how students who have less than stellar academic PSLE or even "O" or "N" level scores often end up doing very well in the polytechnic system.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: They are able to achieve good grade point average scores in the polytechnic, which reflects their ability to do well academically.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: They are transformed from being regarded as academically poor or average, into good academic achievers.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The main difference, of course, is that they are now in a system that measures academic achievement in terms of coursework and skills capability, as opposed to the ability to study for an exam.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: There are some subjects at the "N" and "O" levels that allow students to do well based on their practical and skills-based capabilities, but the fact remains that our education system is still very much an exam-based academic one, especially when it comes to the mother-of-all exams, the PSLE.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The Government has, over the years, increasingly recognised that there are multiple pathways to success.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Having a degree, for example, is only one of the many peaks of excellence and we have, indeed, seen many examples of successful people who do not have degrees.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The fundamental objective of education is thus not to pursue paper qualifications, but the assurance that the receivers of education learn employable and relevant skills that enable them to succeed in the industry or career of their choice.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In an earlier speech debating the President’s Address in May, I briefly commented on how the Government has recognised the importance of providing learners with various options that cater to different learning needs and aspirations in the post-primary school education sector.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The same choices are also given to parents in the pre-primary education sector with different early childhood education options providing different pedagogies and curricula to suit different needs.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I am supportive of Ms Rahayu Mahzam’s amendments that development paths need to be suited to unique strengths and interests and I believe strongly that having different systems and different pathways will ultimately be beneficial as it produces different products.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: A system of this nature must necessarily recognise the potential of each and every learner and create diverse pathways for everyone to meet their potential and aspirations.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In this increasingly complex world, it is not so much about what you know, as what you can do.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I thus strongly urge the Government to consider how we can continue to ensure that our people, both the young and not-so-young, are given adequate opportunities and pathways that allow them to learn and develop along different pathways, while at the same time, master a set of life skills and domain knowledge that enables them to maximise their unique potential.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I always make the comment that we will never presume to tell a lawyer how to do his job.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: You would not go onto a plane to tell a pilot how to fly a plane.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Indeed, you would not tell a brain surgeon how to perform surgery.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: Mr	Speaker, Sir,	I	thank	you	for	allowing	me	to	speak	on	the Motion.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: When	my	colleague	and	fellow	Nominated Member of Parliament,	Asst Prof Mahdev	Mohan, mooted	the	idea	of	a	Motion	that	recognises	and	endorses	the	love	of	learning	as	the	foundation	for	our	future and	that	education should be inclusive,	accessible	and	a	lifelong	experience	for	everyone	in	Singapore,	it	was	a	no-brainer	for	me	to	endorse	and	support	this	meaningful	Motion.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: I	would	also	like	to	preface	my	speech	by	stating	that	the	education	system	in	Singapore	is	a	world-class	system	that	has	done	well	for	our	country and	continues	to	be	a	key	path	of	success	for	those	who	have	less.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: However,	like	any	system,	now	and	again,	there	may	be	a	need	to	take	a	step	back,	every	once	in	a	while,	to	see	if	there	might	be	tweaks	and	adjustments	that	would	ensure	that	a	strong	system	becomes	even	stronger	over	time,	to	keep	up	with	evolving	needs	and	demands.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: In	Singapore,	growing	affluence	and	rising	aspirations are	a	few	among	many	factors	that	point	to	a	need	for	an	even	more	calibrated	approach	to	education.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: Some	may	argue	that	Singapore	is	doing	fine.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: It is	precisely	because	we	are	doing	so	well	that	we	should	take	this	opportunity	to	wholeheartedly	support	things	that	are	working	well	for	Singapore and	perhaps	consider	slight	tweaks	to	areas	that	are	not	functioning	at	their	full	potential.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: In	my	speech	today,	I	will	be	focusing	on	two	main	areas: sports	education	in	Singapore	and the	bigger	role	that	parents	can	play	in	nurturing	the	talents	of	their	children.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: Much	of	it	will	be	through	anecdotes	from	my	experience	as	the	father	of	a	child	who	has	gone	through	sports	education	in	a	local primary school,	as	well	as	from	the	many	conversations	that	I	have	had	with	parents	with	children	in	the	current primary	and secondary school local system.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: Like	many	in	this	House,	my	wife	and	I	enrolled	our	son	in	the	local primary school	system.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: It is	a	system	that	is	robust,	well	thought through and which works.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: While	many	parents	focused	predominantly	on	a	school’s	academic	success,	accessibility	through	alumni	membership or	perhaps	proximity	to	home,	my	wife	and	I,	when	looking	for	a primary school	for	our	son,	also	looked	at	the	breadth	of	sports	offered	by	the	school.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: You	see, Sir,	as	I	have	shared	before	in	this House,	sports	is	not	just	about	fitness,	wellness and	competition.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: More	importantly, Members	in	this	House	who	have	played	sports	would	agree	with	me	here, sports	is	about	learning	traits, such	as	teamwork,	fair	play and	values	such	as	respect,	resilience	and	graciousness.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: Through	sports, children	learn	sportsmanship	and	other	life	skills.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: They	develop	a	sense	of	fellowship	with	one’s	competitiveness	that	is	not	selfish	or	self-centred.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: Sports	would also	enable	our	children	to	build	relationships	with	people	across	all	sectors,	with	many	lasting	a	lifetime.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: On	the	football	pitch,	when	you are	playing	as	a	team,	it	matters	not	whether	you	live	in	a	1-room	rental	flat	or	a	good	class	bungalow,	or	whether	you are	the	top	student	or	worst	student	in	class.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: What	matters	most	is	that	you	are	working	together,	having	each	other’s	back,	in	the	bid	to	score	against	the	opposing	team.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: It is	perhaps	one	of	the	best	social	leveller	platforms	around.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: So, when	it	was	time	to	sign	up	my	son	for	a	sport,	it	was	a	new	experience	for	me.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: Back	in	the	day	when	I	wanted	to	play	a	sport,	I	just	turned	up	when	the	teachers	asked	me	to and	that	was	it, we	played.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: Today,	it is	a	pretty	complicated	exercise	to	play	in	the	sport	of	your	choice.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: This	is	also	incredibly	tough	for	parents	who	do not	have	immediate	access	to	the	Internet	during	that	specific	window.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: I have always	been	puzzled	by	the	thinking	behind	this.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: If	you	are	a	child	in	a primary school and love	a	sport	and	want	to	play	it,	you	should	be	encouraged	to	pursue	your	passion	instead	of	being	told	that	there	are	“not	enough”	places	in	that	CCA	and	sent	off	to	a	sport	or	CCA	that	you	have	absolutely	no	interest	in.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: Often,	we	hear	about	schools	that	decide	against	offering	sports	options	that	they	do	not	excel	in.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: I	know	of	one	particular	school	that	stopped	offering	a	sport	after	repeatedly	finishing	second	and	third	in	national	tournaments.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: Parents	and	children	are	also	told	that	that	there	are	too	few	children	interested	in	that	particular	sport	so	it	does not	make	sense	to	offer	that	CCA.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: The	end	result	is	that	even	if	it is	a	fairly	popular	sport	like	football or	tennis,	some	schools	tend	to	not	offer	the	sport	as	a	CCA.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: You	can	engage	your	own	coach	and	enlist	your	child	in	a	programme	to	participate	in	the	sport	he	or	she	enjoys and, we, as	a	school, will	recognise	it	as	an	official	CCA".

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: It	also	means	that	parents	have	a	very	big	say	in	the	running	of	the	CCA and, sometimes, this	can	lead	to	conflicts	of	interests	with	regard	to	team	selections	and	performance.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: Perhaps, a	solution	would	be	for	schools	in	a	particular	zone	or	area	to	come	together	and	decide	collectively	to	offer	sports	that	they	may	not	be	able	to	offer	on	their	own.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: The	shared fees	would	reduce	the	burden	for	less	affluent	families.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: If	a	child	does	not	know	what	sport	he	or	she	wants	to	participate	in,	the	introduction	to	a	comprehensive	sports	programme, perhaps	during physical education (PE),	will	allow	the	child	to	familiarise	himself	or	herself	with	different	types	of	sports and	identify	ones	that	he	or	she	enjoys and	would	want	to	pursue.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: This	would	also	give	children	a	broader	understanding	of	sports	in	general,	be	it rugby,	football,	swimming,	table	tennis,	badminton, hockey or whatever the sport may be.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: I	understand	that	some	schools	do introduce	one	or	two	sports	during	PE, but	this	is	not	comprehensive, nor	is	it	standard	across	all	schools.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: The	Government	could	also	take	the	lead	in	creating	public	spaces	where	kids	can	play	sports without	the	hassle	of	booking	fields	and	courts, many	of	which	require	some	form	of	online	registration	and	payment,	which	children	might	not	have	access	to.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: We have	done	an	amazing	job	with	our	park	connectors.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: Surely, we	can	do	just	as amazing a job	by	creating	open,	public	spaces	in neighbourhoods	where	any	child	can	play	a	sport	of	his	or	her	choice,	without	fear	of	reproach, meaning, not	being	chased	away	or	reprimanded	as	I	was	decades	ago	when honing	my	football	skills	in	HDB	void	decks.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: For those running sports CCAs, many are former national and club sportsmen who may have robust credentials as sportsmen but have little or no qualification or experience in coaching or, more importantly, educating children.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: I have seen this first-hand, where fundamentals like proper warm-up and warm-down techniques, drills and explanations about sportsmanship and respect are not part of the sports CCA's curriculum.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: What you often find instead is a strong emphasis on winning, which in itself is not a bad thing; but sports education in schools should be more than just about winning.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: There are vendors who blatantly tell parents, "Your child need more coaching.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: I am happy to coach him outside of the CCA hours, and these are my rates".

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: And lo and behold, the kids who go for these private extra coaching end up on the first team representing the school.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: Again, this encourages elitism, where the affluent parents will be able to get their kids on the school team because they can afford the additional coaching.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: There are also vendors who are harassed by parents on the sidelines: parents who yell instructions and abuses during tournaments and pressure the coaches to place their children.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: Again, this is not what playing sport is about.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: Worse still, children who have parents who work lose out because their mothers or fathers are not at the training or competition grounds to lobby on behalf of their children.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: Perhaps, Sport Singapore, the Singapore Sports Institute and the Singapore Sports School can lend their expertise to help schools craft the PE and sports CCA curriculum so that every child can enjoy and reap the benefits of sport.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: Teachers managing sports CCAs as well as vendors could also be better trained to nurture children who play sport, which could include advice on nutrition and physical and mental wellness.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: But I raise this now, in light of this Motion, to strongly urge the House that if we are serious about encouraging our children to pursue their passions, that education continues to be the pathway for success for those who have less, then perhaps it is time that we pay more attention to sports education.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: Sports in our schools should be a meeting place for friendship, fellowship and the pure enjoyment of sport, regardless of your family and financial background.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: It is one of the few places in a child's schooling life where he or she is not judged by their academic prowess and we should do all we can to return to this spirit.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: While the scheme has worked and Minister Ng Chee Meng has announced that a review is being undertaken to address how different schools select students, here are some observations about the scheme that merit further scrutiny.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: Some of them are so good at it that they will refund the fees if your child does not make it to the school of your choice through the DSA programme.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: So, parents who can afford the fees would enrol their kids in these programmes.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: A friend, whose child attended one of these classes, talked about how the coach instructed the child not to pass the ball to his team mates during the trials or when the coaches from the DSA schools were observing him.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: This is to ensure that the child would outshine his team mates and secure that precious DSA place in the school.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: Another child, who had no interest in any sport, was enrolled by his parents into a shooting class that guaranteed success in the DSA trials and a place in a top school.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: Yes, the boy got into the school through DSA, but is now miserable as he does not enjoy the sport and only enrolled and played it to get into the top school.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: We need to ask ourselves if this is what the DSA scheme is intended to be and if this "gaming" of the system is acceptable.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: Do we want to encourage such behaviour and, worse, reward it, by giving these children places in our top schools?

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: What we need is for the system to also recognise and reward children who exemplify good sportsmanship and character as these are qualities that will stay with them beyond their school sporting careers.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: Just look at Japan at this year's Federation Internationale de Football Association (FIFA) World Cup in Russia.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: They were a hair's breadth away from beating Belgium and qualifying for the Quarter Finals but the world now remembers them more for their behaviour off the field, for their fair play and how they left their dressing room spotless and penned a note of thanks in Russian to their hosts.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: Sean, the school's hockey captain, captured our hearts earlier this year when he asked the umpire not to allow a goal that his team had scored when their opponent was not ready, as he felt it would not have been fair to the other team.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: This resulted in his team eventually losing the match.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: To me, values, such as integrity and fair play, are as important, if not more, than one's ability as an athlete.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: Fundamentally, it is up to parents who should know and understand our children best, to make the best decision with them and not for them.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: I think most people in this House know that I love sport.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: I played it at all levels and am a true football nut.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: So, when my son came along, all I dreamed of was to see him have the same passion for sport as I did, and for football, in particular.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: When he was about four or five years old, I enrolled him in a football academy, as I had wanted him to have a very good foundation.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: But after a few weeks of watching him from the sidelines, I noticed that while he seemed happy enough, instead of going after the ball and passing it, all he seemed to do was chase after the other children, much like he was playing a game of "catching".

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: So, on the way home from training one day, I decided to have a heart-to-heart with him. "Do you actually enjoy football?" I asked. "Yes, daddy, very much", he said, smiling.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: Then, I pressed, "But why do you just chase the kids around?" The smile on his face turned to a frown and, almost bursting into tears, he said, "Actually, daddy, I don't like football at all." So, I said, "Why didn't you say anything, you don't have to play the sport if you don't like it?" And his response broke my heart, "Because you love football, daddy." That is when I realised that, as a father, I just assumed that my child would love what I loved and would want to be just like me.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: But I had never bothered to ask him what he liked.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: So, for the next few years, we encouraged him to play whatever sport or activity he wanted.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: He tried everything from aikido, to swimming to table tennis to golf.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: And, finally, after a few years later, on his own, he began to develop a love for football – thank God!

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: And he is today an accomplished footballer, having played competitive football for school and club.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: It is a sport he genuinely loves, for all the right reasons.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: As parents, it is natural to want our children to be just like us and have the same interests as us.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: As a parent, it is also easy to fall into the trap of seeing other parents and their children succeeding and excelling in different sports and thinking to ourselves our boy or girl could also do that.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: I know of parents who have pushed their children so hard that their children end up resenting not just the sport but their parents as well.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: I am reminded of an interview I read in the Financial Times about a month ago.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: It was an interview with Andira Zafirakou, who was recently crowned the best teacher in the world, the 2018 winner of the Global Teacher Prize.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: She says and I quote, "Every child is different.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: Some children will really benefit from the military lining up and find it comforting.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: (In Tamil):  : 	Mr Speaker, sports in schools are not just for ordinary physical exercise.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: Neither is it for the purpose of competition.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: Children enjoy the benefits of playing in the field through their interaction with one another and learn values, such as comradeship, hard work, discipline and honesty.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: When children engage themselves in sports, they develop among them the sense of competition, become unenvious, forbearing, develop together good virtues and the sense of accepting defeat.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: At present, sports in schools have become very competitive.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: Parents and educators should look into this and create an interest among children for sports and let them enjoy it.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: When the recess bell is rung, the children run and play with one another.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: Likewise, such a situation should exist when they engage themselves in sports activities in schools.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I suspend the Sitting and will take the Chair at 4.20 pm.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Sitting accordingly suspended at 3.58 pm until 4.20 pm.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Education is the key enabler to unleashing potential and poverty; it is the key to gaining more knowledge; and it is the key to staying relevant and future-ready.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: The Motion on Education is a broad topic.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: I just wish to speak on something that is close to my heart: adult learning and lifelong learning.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Continuous skills upgrading and learning are paramount for us to keep abreast of the changes that are happening in the fast-changing world.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: The SkillsFuture credit was introduced to encourage Singaporeans to learn new skills, new knowledge.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Some use it for higher learning programmes and, some others, for new skills.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: However, more awareness needs to be created about the use of this credit.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Additionally, there must be three "Flex" for lifelong learning to be successful.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Flex-time, flex-place, and flex-learning would further encourage Singaporeans to embrace lifelong learning more readily.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: What is important is the tenacity to be open-minded, be adaptable to un-learn and re-learn new knowledge and skill sets.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: There should be co-ownership between employers and employees and interns to train and learn, so that employers can retain skilled people in the workforce.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Employees must be open to training and upgrading their skills and knowledge.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Employers should give these employees opportunities to go for training so as to upskill themselves.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: More online learning courses can be made available to allow for flexibility in learning.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: The winning formula for continuous and lifelong learning is mindset change by all three parties.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Employers must be receptive to training young people through effective collaboration with Institutes of Higher Learning (IHLs) and increase the rate of place-and-train for students, interns and employees.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Employees, too, must be receptive to the notion of learning while working and with attaining a skill qualification or equivalent skills.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: The Government, too, must change its mindset towards the definition of training and learning.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: In today's time and age, learning is multifaceted and the mode of learning is multi-pronged.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: It need not be purely classroom training of defined hours, but rather, a composite type of training which includes classroom, on-the-job training, application-based learning, e-learning and, in some cases, virtual reality, too, can be used.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: SkillsFuture Singapore, too, must transform to meet the needs of today's industry and training relevance.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: The ideal is to have WSQ programmes for skill-based training.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: However, if the regulatory and policy process becomes an impediment to making a relevant customised programme nationally recognised, then we have a challenge of persuading both young and mature workers to go for training recognised only within the company.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Skill sets must be transferable, even though this can be customised.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: We need to be agile and yet develop programmes to fit the need of industries of not only today, but for the future.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: The question of how fast do the IHLs develop programmes that are relevant for the future, as identified by EDB, which brings in new investments, remains to be seen.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: For instance, in the green energy industry sector, have we trained an adequate number of cohorts to fit this industry under the place-and-train programme, if we find that this will be the future-ready skill that is required now?

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: If data analytics and AI are expected of future industries, the future workforce, how ready are we in developing our own skilled workforce?

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Can the IHLs turn this around to suit the needs of the future fast enough?

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: It also suggested they scored higher on test anxiety.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: This rate is for a population of 15 years of age and above, who can, with understanding, read and write simple statements in their everyday life.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Such achievements are commendable, but it has to translate into a better life for Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: It is, indeed, heartening to note the Education Minister Ong Ye Kung's comment in a recent The Straits Times interview, "Singapore's compass for the education system points towards two things: preparing the young for the future and ensuring that education continues to be an uplifting and integrating force in society".

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: In other words, education is a social leveller.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: His comments provide a new hope and the beginning of a new dawn to those who have missed out on their formal education route.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: He further stressed that Singaporeans should not narrow their opportunities by chasing only after paper qualifications and pursuing academic excellence, such as going to university.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: It is important not to place over-emphasis on academic achievements, but on skills and talents.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: We must embrace diversity of skills and talents, each of which combines to form a successful Singapore, since human resource is our only available critical asset and brain power is our gift.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Employers should not recruit based on paper qualifications alone, but to look at other skill sets relevant to the job.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Many employers are still taking examination grades as proxy to a potential employee doing well at work.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Education should not be exclusive to a few, but an inclusive social leveller.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: We must transform the way we teach and the way we learn and discover new things.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: For continuous learning and lifelong learning to be successful, there must be conversations with adult learners and working people, as many are attending part-time classes to attain paper qualifications.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: In fact, some private sectors are more inclined to recruit an applicant based on skill sets and this is, indeed, commendable.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Recently, I met with a union member who asked, "If I do part-time studies, will I receive additional increment or job promotion once I pass or graduate from this programme?" This is a natural reaction of anyone who wants to upgrade himself or herself.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: For lifelong learning to really succeed, one must erase the notion of "establish reward first, then train", but learn and train for the love of learning and staying relevant.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: This can be done with the Singapore Conversation.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: In summary, learning must be enjoyable, interesting, flexible and innovative, so as to capture the attention of both the young and old.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: We can catalyse the love for lifelong learning by forming a community of learners and a lifelong learning movement, especially when a person transits from school to workplace and this has to be seamless.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Education itself must be inclusive and be deemed as a social leveller to break the cycle of poverty.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: I declare my interest as President of the Society for the Physically Disabled (SPD) and board member of SG Enable.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: For this speech, I acknowledge SPD, Singapore Association of Occupational Therapists (SAOT) and Dr May Lim Sok Mui of the Singapore Institute of Technology (SIT) for their professional inputs.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: Any unpalatable views, however, are entirely my own.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: We are naturally drawn to and congregate with people who, overall, are like us and who possess qualities that we aspire to have.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: It is, therefore, not natural for us to embrace people who are different or who face challenges or difficulties that we do not want for ourselves.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: It is difficult to be different from the majority.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: Disabilities and special needs make us different from the majority – the way we look, the way we walk, the way we talk, the way we think.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: All these make us different in different aspects and it is difficult for us.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: Inclusive education is, therefore, necessary because of differences and can only succeed by design.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: First, we must be careful not to place the interest of one group of students above the other.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: The interests of both groups are equally important.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: We should, to the extent practicable, remove barriers against children accepting one another.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: They are also given the opportunity to develop meaningful friendships, understand, appreciate and respect individual differences and prepare for engagement in diversity.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: Therefore, inclusive education, if prudently implemented, benefits children with and without disabilities.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: From the broader and long-term perspective, inclusive education forges a common identity and bonding between our young ones, with and without disabilities or special needs, and inculcates in them important values, all of which will, in turn, build their resilience and that of our country.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: The provision of accessible infrastructure, where children are brought together in common physical spaces creates opportunities for shared experiences and the sharing of diverse experiences, just like in National Service, and that, in turn, creates a common bonding.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
