text: The setting of special classes in mainstream schools allows students with special needs to spend some of their lessons in special education classes appropriate to them and also in other classes together with their non-special education peers.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: Thirdly, of course, which is also what is happening now, the inclusion of students with disabilities or special needs in mainstream schools.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: Perhaps, the Ministry of Education (MOE) can also consider a concept of enhancing a common identity through the wearing of the same uniform.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: So, when schools co-locate or where they have sharing of classes, perhaps the students could wear the same uniform.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: That way, they will feel like they are one and the same, together in the environment that they will grow together in.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: The third principle, removing what keeps students apart.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: The first sub-principle is to increase their independence.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: When we broadly categorise school activities into learning, self-care and school-leisure, it becomes apparent that children with handwriting difficulties, cerebral palsy, autism spectrum disorder, attention deficit hyperactive disorder, social and emotional issues and so on, will find difficulties engaging in these school activities.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: Such difficulties will create dependency on teachers and classmates and will impede the performance to the full potential of the child.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: In addition, the dependency on teachers and classmates could result in the child being perceived as a source of nuisance, annoyance or disruption.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: If we drop a pen, we can pick it up rather easily.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: So, it is understandable that we may be annoyed if we have to repeatedly pick up a pen for a student or a classmate.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: The difficulties in engaging in school activities are intimidating, but not insurmountable.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: The use of assistive technology, environmental modification, application of principles of Universal Design for Learning (UDL) and life/social skills development can overcome or ameliorate the difficulties.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: However, expertise in these areas lies outside that of our teachers.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: It is not reasonable to expect teachers to be occupational therapists, physiotherapists, speech therapists, IT experts, social workers and counsellors, all at once.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: And, yet, the current support system for students in these respects is limited by structural and funding constraints.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: So, we have limited access to occupational therapists because it is on an ad hoc and time-limited basis.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: Organisations like SAOT and SPD that provide a suite of relevant professional services to support schools are not often called upon.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: We may facilitate learning in three ways: through the adoption of UDL in which teachers and educators are guided in the development of flexible learning curriculum which caters to the individual learning differences of students, whether with or without disabilities or special needs.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: For example, instead of delivering an essay, students may be assessed on a video produced by them.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: And the UDL framework accommodates students, regardless of needs, right from the start.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: Next, to be open to the development of bespoke curriculum that caters to the abilities of the children, taking into consideration their disabilities or special needs.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: So, we base the curriculum on the national curriculum, but modify that according to the abilities or disabilities of a child.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: And we issue the certifications for the completion of the courses accordingly.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: Next, we could work on the better adoption of technology through the use of real-time, interactive, direct-to-classroom virtual learning.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: We could also use mainstream voice-to-text or text-to-voice technology for a child who is unable to type or not able to see or not able to hear.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: This technology can empower them to do their homework, to hear a book, even to do their examinations.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: If you would like to know more, please visit Tech Able.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: In Australia, school-level good practices include adjustments to cultures, policies and practices, development of support structures, regimes of funding support and the provision of and access to equitable learning opportunities.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: In class, differentiating curriculum or alternative curricula, application of universal design, use of information technologies and individual education plans are applied for students.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: In addition, the cultural change in the school shows that it takes a whole school to make the students with disabilities feel welcome and accepted.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: Inclusive education turns very much on acceptance by Singaporeans of persons with disabilities and special needs.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: Inclusive education requires parents of children without disabilities and special needs to agree and encourage their children to make friends with children with disabilities, to allow children with disabilities and special needs to attend school with them.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: It also requires educators and policymakers to be bold, affirming that education goes beyond the acquisition of knowledge to the inculcation of values, the most basic of which is the respect for the dignity and potential of another human being and, by so affirming, to walk the talk.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: I understand MSF is taking action to resource preschools and I applaud that.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: But consistent with these findings, the findings on mainstream primary school enrolment are that half of the parents of children with special needs consider it a success if their children can get into a mainstream primary school.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: Inclusive education requires members of the public to accept people with disabilities and children with disabilities.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: Based on survey findings, whilst 64% of Singaporeans are willing to share public spaces with people with disabilities, they are not willing to interact with them.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: All these mindsets will filter down to the young souls of our children.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: Unless we change, our children cannot be any better.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: So, I ask that we all work together.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: And parents of children with disabilities, I ask that you do not give up.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: Your struggles may be phenomenal, but you do not have to walk alone because there are many Singaporeans who will walk with you.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: In my concluding remarks, Sir, I want to say again that it is difficult to be different from the majority.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: Our disabilities and special needs make us different from the majority.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: And the differences are accentuated when we are placed in environments that are suited to the majority.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: In a short story written by HG Wells, "The Country of the Blind", a fully sighted mountaineer named Nuñez loses his way and finds himself in the "Country of the Blind".

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: It is an unusual village with windowless houses and a network of paths, all bordered by kerbs.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: He thinks, that in the "Country of the Blind", the One-Eyed Man is King.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: The villagers cannot, however, understand the concept of sight because they live in darkness.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: In due course, he falls in love with his employer's daughter but he is not allowed to marry her, unless his eyes are removed.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: It depends on the version that you want to read.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: But we learn that the differences arise from different perspectives.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: In the Country of the Blind, who is the person with a disability?

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: We can all work together and turn differences and different perspectives into positive effect, only if we hear each other and are prepared to push frontiers unfamiliar to us.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: So, when I did not do my homework, I was punished.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: When I talked too much, I was punished.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: It was not always easy; there were times when I felt like a burden.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: It got easier when I went to university.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: My principal was here yesterday, she was one of those who accommodated me.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: Our education strategy must continue to be founded on the basis of a love for learning.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: I believe, however, that we should also not neglect the role that economic priorities have had in shaping the choices that we have made in this area both as a society as well as individuals.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: It is important to recognise that the ultimate satisfaction that individuals derive from learning is often based as much on the fulfilment of practical objectives as it is on philomathean impulses.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: In an age of intensifying global and regional economic competition, there is almost no doubt that the economic imperatives determining what we learn, how we learn and where we learn will only continue to grow in dominance.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: We should see the education journey of our nation in the light of the challenges we have faced in building our nation.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: There are many of these, most notably those in OECD.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: Supporting individuals in their pursuit of a love of learning cannot be allowed to become identified with a denial of the importance of pursuing practical economic value in the learning process.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: Both should be seen as alternate perspectives of the enrichment of human capital for the individual.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: For a small country like Singapore whose dependence on workforce performance is now being brought into sharp relief with the simultaneous onslaught of demographic shifts, skills challenges and productivity concerns, ensuring the human capital security of future generations of workers should be of paramount concern to policymakers.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: By ensuring we maximise the human capital potential of our small workforce, we can continue to overcome the natural disadvantages of being a small nation competing at the frontiers of technology.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: The education system we have has been holding out the best hope for expanding opportunities for the disadvantaged and one of the main challenges we face is to ensure this continues to remain so in the face of the disruptive forces that unsettle both our economy and our society.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: Since Independence, Singapore’s education system has enabled widespread participation with its strong emphasis on ensuring universal access to basic education.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: This approach has brought tangible benefits to large segments of society.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: In particular, members of the lower-income groups have been able to take advantage of significant opportunities for social mobility.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: Hence, the relevance of this Motion to the lower income is especially important.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: This should bring us back to the fundamental basis of the early success of our system.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: This is a recognition of the fact that should the opportunities to this group narrow, the overall outcomes to society will worsen.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: One of the most prominent empirical economic findings in the last few decades has been the determination that the estimated impact that additional years of schooling have on tangible labour market outcomes, especially earnings, is a significant measurable magnitude.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: In anticipation of this payoff, there has been a change in behaviour and that is the reason why we have witnessed huge individual and societal investments in educational pursuits.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: The education system must ensure that all segments of society have access that enables them to gain from these payoffs in a manner that at least matches their efforts.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: The data on the employment outcomes of graduates from tertiary institutions in Singapore confirm these points.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: Nothing emphasises the importance of educational attainment more than the fact that university graduates, generally speaking, earn more than their polytechnic counterparts.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: This shows that even as further education bestows clear advantages in the labour market, the benefits are not confined to further education at the university level alone.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: This is particularly important for social mobility, for it demonstrates the availability of intermediate levels of upgrading which do not prevent those with limited means – financial or otherwise – from attaining the same educational goals as those who are better endowed or better resourced.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: Nonetheless, compelling as they are, starting salaries represent only part of the picture about how well any system of education performs.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: It is important to also consider how well an educational foundation serves its graduates over the span of their careers.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: The major challenge posed by the rapid advance of technology is the accelerating pace at which knowledge and skills become obsolete.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: The need to make up for the natural depletion of knowledge is not a concept that is foreign to this House.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: Members of this House, at various points in the last few years, have shown a keen understanding of this connection.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: During the Committee of Supply (COS) debate for the Ministry of Trade and Industry in 1994, for instance, Assoc Prof Koo Tsai Kee, then-Member for Tanjong Pagar, had argued that there was a link between the fact that "the shelf life of knowledge is becoming shorter and shorter" and the need to treat education and training as "continuous lifelong processes".

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: Again, in 2005, during the COS debate for MOE, then-nominated Member of Parliament, Dr Loo Choon Yong, had warned that "even medical knowledge has a half-life of seven years only".

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: A year and a half after that, during the debate on the President's Address, the Minister of State for Trade and Industry at that time, Mr Lee Yi Shyan, in pushing for a re-examination of the skills upgrading policy then, had pointed out that "half of what you learn in four years in polytechnics and universities can become obsolete in two years, and they get halved every two years".

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: Much more recently, just this year, during the debate on the Annual Budget Statement, our hon colleague Mr Patrick Tay drew our attention to the issue of skills being at risk.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: There is already good appreciation about the importance of continuous learning.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: And there is also widespread acknowledgement that such continuous learning, regardless of whether we speak of lifelong educational pursuits, retraining at work or continuous upgrading of skills, is thrust upon us by the advance of technology and the resulting decline in the shelf life of knowledge and skills.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: Adult learners have to juggle different roles and the immediacy of their roles in the workforce means that their skills must be responsive to current employer needs.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: The system of skills training and upgrading should be built upon a firm foundation imbued in young learners from an early age that learning itself must always be a lifelong pursuit.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: The importance of learning takes on added prominence during the current industry transformation drive.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: And the sense of uncertainty pervades not just the adult training landscape but also affects the sense of direction of young learners, many of whom are often confused about how they should embark upon seemingly irrevocable decisions about lifelong careers at an early age.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: The last thing we want is for everyone to discard the strong foundations currently offered by our education system.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: Learning is age-dependent and young learners benefit from the security of a rigorous grounding in the basics.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: Having a solid foundation in the basics also prepares them for self-directed learning throughout the rest of their lifelong journey as a learner.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: Hence, while we seek to continually upgrade and keep our education system relevant, we must also seek to retain those fundamental pillars of strength which continue to have a timeless relevance for any learner.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: Although there is much scope for policy to promote learning which meets the needs of an advanced economy like ours, the ultimate motivating factor for effective learning is still a love for it.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: That is why it is important to ensure that policies are an enabler, helping learners to persist in their natural inclination to pursue lifelong learning.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: In closing, Mr Speaker, Sir, I would like to give you my response to the two questions you asked.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: In my opinion, the most important school is the School of Life and that is why I think the most important type of learning is lifelong learning.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: My most important teachers have been all of my teachers.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: In closing, Sir, I would like to take this opportunity to also thank MOE for its tireless efforts in bringing us to this point of our nation-building journey.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: By most measures, we have an excellent education system and our system has kept up with the times and our nation's needs.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: To meet tomorrow's needs, I would like to propose fine-tuning the way we evaluate our students.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Doing so will strengthen the critical thinking and the relevance of what our students learn in the humanities and applied subjects, at the "N", "O" and "A" levels.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: At the same time, I would like to speak about encouraging better social mixing between students from different schools so that we can shape a better future for Singapore.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: In any education system, the evaluation system – or examinations – is the critical link between what should be taught verses what ends up being taught.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: An examination is where the rubber hits the road.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: The best intention of any curriculum developer can only be translated to effective learning if the examinations are properly designed and evaluated correctly by somebody appropriately trained.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Today, our current systems work very well for mathematics and science subjects, because these subjects are objective and theoretical.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Nevertheless, there is scope for fine-tuning in two areas: one, fine-tune how we evaluate humanities subjects; and, two, accredit the industries to evaluate applied subjects.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: From time to time, we sometimes hear that we can do more to promote critical thinking when our students learn humanities.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Some humanities teachers, I was told, teach the students to recognise patterns and regurgitate pre-determined answers.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Well, the humanities study the human condition, society and culture.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Just like in life, there is no right or wrong answer in the humanities.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: There is only a way to think rationally and look at the big picture.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: If we do not teach this, we are doing a disservice to our students and are holding them back beyond their school years.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Why then are some teachers still focused on encouraging students to regurgitate answers, rather than to think critically and independently?

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: One contributing factor could be the way in which our humanities are being marked at the "O", "N" and "A" levels.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Currently, overseas educators from Cambridge mark our examination papers.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: They then provide annual feedback to MOE on how our students fare.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: In addition, every few years, the Cambridge chief markers will come down to Singapore to provide in-depth feedback to selected Singapore teachers under the "train-the-trainer" approach.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: These Singapore teachers then relay the gist of what they have learnt from the Cambridge markers to the rest of the teachers.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: However, because information is sometimes lost in the transmission process, some of the Singapore humanities teachers might not get a uniform picture of how Cambridge evaluates our students.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: And some of these teachers, operating without the fullest clarity and, I must stress, out of the best intention for their students, fall back on encouraging pattern recognition and regurgitation of pre-determined answers.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: If this is a possible issue, then a possible solution must be to try to provide as much clarity as possible to our teachers.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: But I hope that once they become markers, they should not be allowed to go back to become teachers or part-time tutors.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Besides focusing on marking, they can also work closely and strengthen MOE's curriculum development team.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: And because this team is based in Singapore rather than in Cambridge, they will have ample time to communicate with full clarity with all our Singapore-based teachers.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Because our teachers will have minimal uncertainty on how the markers will grade the subjects, our curriculum developers will have more opportunities to: one, promote independent thinking; and, two, shorten the curriculum review cycle.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: At the same time, it will ensure a clear divide between the professional markers and the teachers, so that the markings can continue to be fair and equitable.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Next, I would like to talk about applied subjects.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: I am very heartened by the recent moves to teach applied subjects, such as computing, mobile robotics, sports science and retail operations at the "N", "O" and "A" levels.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: This is a good move that can prepare our students for the future and I believe we can build on this.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: We can do so in two ways: one, by ensuring our students are taught the most current curriculum; and, two, by ensuring our students are being evaluated by accredited examiners with directly relevant industry experience.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: As we know, in some applied subjects, changes in technology happen quickly and a six-to-eight year curriculum cycle could be too long.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Of course, one can argue that at the "N", "O" and "A" levels, our students can focus on the foundational knowledge for applied courses.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Nevertheless, there could be scope for us to do better.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: One way we can do so is to examine what is being done in Hong Kong.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: I am not advocating for our examination board to be privatised like in Hong Kong.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: I do understand this is a departure from the current way we evaluate, but I hope that we can at least explore incorporating elements of this approach even for our "N", "O" and "A" levels.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Related to this is to encourage more industry practitioners to join in as teachers or as part-time teachers for applied subjects.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Today, I believe that we have a lot of capable industry practitioners who are teaching and lecturing at universities and they find it a privilege to do so.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Perhaps we could also confer the same amount of prestige and encouragement to encourage more of these industry practitioners, very excellent industry practitioners, to do so in ITE and polytechnics as well.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Working with the industry to be accredited examiners, bringing more industry practitioners to be teachers, these two will help our students learn current content for applied subjects and help us transit towards a model that is closer to Germany's apprenticeship model.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Even though our social divide is nowhere as serious as in many other countries, there is always scope for us to do better.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: MOE is already doing a lot, but there could be scope for more.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: MOE can also strengthen the collaboration with the Ministry of Culture, Community and Youth (MCCY)'s ActiveSG to encourage social mixing through sports.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Today, MCCY is already encouraging students to interact with their peers doing sports outside of their school.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: These are just two ideas where MOE can encourage our youth to come together to bridge the social divides.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: When our youth willingly come together to socialise, they will treasure the bonds that they built.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: To sum up what I have suggested, education is not preparing students for examinations.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: By strengthening the teaching of independent and critical thinking, up-to-date practical skills and social skills, we can further achieve our aim.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: With that, Mr Speaker, I support the Motion.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Many of you spoke passionately and many from personal experiences, especially Ms Rahayu Mahzam, whom I also thank for proposing additions to the Motion, which I support.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Senior Parliamentary Secretary Assoc Prof Faishal Ibrahim and Second Minister Indranee Rajah will address many of the issues raised by Members.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Amidst all the ideas and suggestions raised, I thought it will be useful for me to speak on the key principles of Singapore's education system.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Last week, David Brooks wrote a piece called, "The paradox of the gender divide".

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: He observed that in the Nordic countries, where gender equality is the highest, many women exercise their choice and opt out of the corporate rat race.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: So, the greater the gender equality, the fewer the number of female corporate managers.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: It encourages us to develop our talents and put our talents and strengths to good use.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: This approach has uplifted many families over the decades.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Many Members of the House have benefited from this approach and philosophy.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: And as families do well, they believe in meritocracy and, therefore, they spare no effort investing in their next generation, including enrichment classes, from a very young age.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Hence, children today from more affluent families are now doing better than those from lower-income families in school.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Unlike the first generation of Singaporeans where students are mostly from humble backgrounds, the next generation is pushing off blocks from different starting points and students from affluent families have a head start.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: So, meritocracy, arising from a belief in fairness, seems to have, paradoxically, resulted in systematic unfairness.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: This is the question we all ask ourselves.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: There is a second paradox and that is of inequality.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: When I was young, most of my classmates, including myself, were from humble backgrounds.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: By the sheer law of probability, some of us ended up as top performers in schools.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Today, the percentage of students from similar backgrounds are much smaller and it continues to shrink.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: And I think it will continue to shrink as we continue to uplift families.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: But as we successfully uplift more poor families, the smaller group of families that remain poor are facing increasingly difficult challenges.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Their challenges are also translated to their children's performances in school.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: So, as we uplift poor families, the greater the achievement gap between the rich and poor in school.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: As we confront these paradoxes, we question if our policies and approaches have run their course and perhaps it is time to slaughter some sacred cows and take a fundamentally different approach.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: It depends on which cows you are thinking of slaughtering.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Paradoxes make us think hard about our challenges and our choices.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Take the gender divide debate in the Nordic countries.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: They provided more equal opportunities to men and women, but women chose not to be like men and, so, there is no contradiction in both greater equality and fewer female corporate managers.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: How do we deal with the two paradoxes I mentioned: that of meritocracy, and that of achievement gap?

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: It is in danger, recently, of becoming a dirty word.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: A couple of education-related controversies arose in the US recently.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The first was a lawsuit filed against University of Harvard for systemic bias against Asians over the years.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: It was alleged that Asians who tended to score highest in the admission tests for Harvard were marked down by the university on soft criteria, such as personality.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: So, it is not just Singaporeans who are kiasu and study a lot.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Asians overseas, like those in the US, they, too, study very well and ace their examinations.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Apparently, Harvard did this to preserve ethnic diversity in the university.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The second controversy was that the Mayor of New York recently suggested to scrap the highly competitive admission examinations for eight of the city’s specialised public high schools.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Sixty-two percent of the students in these schools are Asians, who tend to perform well in these examinations.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The move by the Mayor of New York will reduce the number of Asians and increase the number of black and Hispanic students being admitted into these specialised high schools.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Some ideas that we have come across in recent weeks – I must say not from this House, but from what we have read – are along the lines of what the US schools are doing.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: There was a suggestion that we set a quota for lower-income students in popular schools.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: I am not in a position to comment on the admission policies for US schools.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: But Singapore’s circumstances are different and unique, and we cannot assume that we will have to eventually do what other countries like the US have done.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Many of our popular schools, and I think Asst Prof Mohan has mentioned it, are making extra efforts to attract eligible students from lower-income families, encouraging diversity amongst students and mingling of students from different backgrounds.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: I do not think it is aligned to our societal ethos.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Another common suggestion that was raised is to scrap the Primary School Leaving Examination (PSLE), one of the sacred cows.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: I will admit that the PSLE is far from a perfect system and does add stress, a lot of stress sometimes – to parents and students.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: But it happens to be the most meritocratic and probably the fairest of all imperfect systems.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: If we scrap it, whatever we replace it with to decide on secondary school postings, I think is likely to be worse.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: I was in Switzerland last month; the Swiss do not have the equivalent of PSLE.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: But neither do students have a choice on what secondary school to go to or work towards to go to.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: They are simply assigned to the school nearest to their homes.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: I visited one of these schools; I spoke to the students and they all go home for lunch because they said it is a five- to 10-minute walk, different directions, and then they come back to school.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: They did not have a choice where to go to.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: However, in Switzerland, the affluent have a choice, because they can pay for their children to go to private schools.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: In Switzerland, 7% of students attend private schools.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: They did away with their equivalent of PSLE some years ago.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: In its place, Hong Kong uses the school examination scores for Primary 5 and 6 to decide on secondary school postings.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: But because different primary schools have different standards, they have come up with a device and a tool to harmonise and to normalise the standards, so that they are comparable.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: In this case, the stress is somewhat transferred upstream.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: And, like the Swiss, there is also a thriving private school sector in Hong Kong, which accounts for nearly 30% of the student intake.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The Chinese Development Assistance Council (CDAC), a self-help group which I chair, has a programme called the supervised Homework Group programme.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Here, young volunteers spend a few hours a week tutoring and helping students from lower-income families with their homework.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: On surface, it is to help these students with their homework, but the unspoken objective is for the volunteers to act as role models for the children.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: I thought the volunteers would be a very suitable group who should have their opinion heard.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: So, I asked if they think PSLE should be scrapped.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: They have no vested interests; they have gone through the education system themselves and they are now helping poor students cope with schoolwork.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The common reasons they cite were that they felt that PSLE can, in fact, motivate the poorer students to work hard and there are resources to support the poorer students.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: One expressed, frankly, that we can complain that PSLE favours the rich, but the rich are better poised to prepare their children in whatever alternate system that is in place.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: They say support the weaker students more, but do not take away the PSLE.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: So, I think it is not a straightforward matter.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Make it less of a do-or-die examination that is so important as if it will determine your whole life, which it does not.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: And there must be many other ways that we can do to reduce the stakes of this examination.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: One way is to ensure a broader definition of merit.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: One that does not focus too narrowly on past academic scores, but recognises a broad meritocracy of skills, given the various strengths and talents of our people.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: That, at the core, is the objective of SkillsFuture.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: That is why pedagogy is changing in schools, which many Members have acknowledged.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: There are many more pathways in the higher education sector, leading into lifelong learning that Assoc Prof Randolph Tan talked about.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We cannot change the fact that the starting point of each child is different, but our system can ensure that all of them can run a good race and finish this well.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Let us talk about the second paradox, the achievement gap.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The easiest way to close the gap is to cap the top.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Some of the suggestions raised in public, such as banning tuition and enrichment classes, redistributing resources from popular to less popular schools, are pointing in that direction.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Excessive tuition to the point of causing undue stress and killing the joy of learning is not good for the child.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: But I do not think capping achievements and limiting opportunities are the right approach either.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: It runs against a very fundamental philosophy of our education system.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: As the educators in MOE will say in Chinese,"保底不封顶", meaning "do not cap the top, but uplift the bottom".

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: And there are many others with great non-academic strengths and talents.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We must continue to strive to help them develop their strengths to the fullest.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The next highest levels of resourcing, about $20,000 and $15,000 per student, goes to Normal (Technical) and Normal (Academic) streams respectively.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: A student in other courses in Government and Government-aided schools and in Independent Schools attracts under $15,000 of resources per student.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: In addition, MOE regularly rotates and ensures that our good performing teachers and principals are well spread across different types of schools.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Beyond resourcing of schools, further assistance is granted to students from lower-income households in the form of financial assistance schemes, bursaries, school meal programmes and the Opportunity Fund.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The Public Service Commission (PSC) also reaches out to students from different schools, in a quest for diversity amongst Government scholars.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: It has been paying special attention to applicants from lower-income families.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Students from two junior colleges (JCs) – Raffles Institution (RI) and Hwa Chong – used to dominate the scholarships awards.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: They recognise that students from poorer backgrounds tend to be less articulate.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: So, the Commission is assessing candidates beyond their communication skills, but instead, looking into the substance of what they say, their ideas and thinking.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: As a result, we continue to see President’s Scholars who come from humble backgrounds or outside the most popular JCs.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: In 2016, LTA Natasha Ann Lum Mei Seem became the first President’s and Singapore Armed Forces Scholar from Pioneer JC.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: She is now studying in the US and is an Air Force C3 Officer.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: At last year’s President’s Scholar award ceremony, I sat next to Mr Lee Tat Wei, whose father was a taxi driver and mother a part-time sales assistant.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Tat Wei is also studying in the US and, when he graduates, he will join the Foreign Service.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Our approach of lifting the bottom has other significant outcomes.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: First, what we used to regard as opportunities available to students from more affluent backgrounds are now broadly accessible.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: For example, most schools now organise overseas learning experiences.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Schools are offering a wide variety of CCAs: Tanglin Secondary School has fencing as a CCA; Kent Ridge Secondary School offers sailing, North Vista Secondary School offers string ensemble and NorthLight School has, for many years, run an equestrian programme for its students.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The Junior Sports Academy (JSA) is another example.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: It is a two-year free sports development programme for talented and interested P4 and P5 students.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The Academy does not scout for high-performing athletes and sportsmen and sportswomen; they look for raw diamonds, students with good motor skills and hand-eye coordination abilities and then help them develop their sporting skills through professional coaching.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Some students from the Programme – and Mr Rajaram may be happy to note this – have gone on to gain places in secondary schools through the Direct School Admission (DSA) system.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: They did not go to those expensive coaches with high rates.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: It is done by the JSA and is free-of-charge.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: MOE is now in the initial stages of developing a similar programme for the Arts.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: It is a good example of an alternate system that we discussed and what will happen if we do not have PSLE.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Mr Rajaram has correctly pointed out, the affluent will always have a way, whatever system it is, to make use of it.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: But in this case, DSA also serves those from humble backgrounds and we are able to train them to enter the top and popular schools.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: So, we ask ourselves: are we better off with, or without, this alternate system?

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: And I think we may well be better off having a system that can enable students from humble backgrounds to enter popular schools, notwithstanding affluent students will also be able to make use of it.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The second significant outcome is smaller class sizes for weaker students.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The additional resources for Specialised Schools and students in Normal streams come partly in the form of additional teaching resources.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: In lower primary, Learning Support Programmes are done in groups of eight to 10.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Many Normal (Technical) classes are now taught in sizes of 20 or have a class size of 40 but two teachers.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: In many JCs, consultations between students and teachers are often one-to-one.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: For sessions with an education and career guidance counsellor, students meet one-on-one or in very small groups.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: There is, sometimes, still the perception that students study in one class and it is of a certain size.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The reality and the lived experience of students are that they now regularly move around, join different groups and there is no single class size.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Our teachers can attest to that through first-hand experience.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: In fact, I think there was a suggestion by Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin to do a study.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: With good teachers, smaller class sizes help the students.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Why then is MOE cautious on the issue of class size?

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Because how it is implemented makes all the difference.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: They are done overseas, but, nevertheless, are scientific studies and we should take note of the results.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: In 2009, Hong Kong did a study on small class teaching in primary schools.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: It put about 700 classes through an experiment over three years, varying their class sizes along the way.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The study found that however they varied the class sizes, there were no significant differences on performances, compared to the territory-wide averages.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: What Hong Kong did find was that where an experimental school or class did significantly better, it was because the principal was more experienced, took an active role in developing the curriculum and the teachers and involved the parents in education.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Those were the key drivers of better performances.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Another study was done by the Taub Center for Social Policy Studies in Israel and results were published in their 2016 Annual Report.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Unlike the Hong Kong study, the Taub Center did not conduct an experiment.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: They gathered a large volume of data on students' results and did a multivariate analysis on the key determinants of the results, with a special focus to find out if class size made a difference.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: There are various explanations behind this, but I would not go into it today.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: One reason was that in the US' context, smaller class sizes meant hiring of many new teachers who were inexperienced and yet to be effective in the classroom.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: But class size reduction policies generally take exactly the opposite approach by pursuing across the board reduction… (They are) also extremely expensive and represented wasted opportunities to make smarter educational investments." When I was in Finland earlier this year, I visited a secondary school.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: And I asked the teachers for their opinion on class sizes.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: They told me this: they said there are different political parties in Finland and each has a position on the class size.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Whoever is elected would then legislate the class size and put it into law.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The teachers said they would rather not have the rigidity.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Earlier generations of Singaporeans have worked hard to uplift their lives and education played a major role.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The doubts of many Singaporeans – whether meritocracy still works, whether inequality is worsening – are, paradoxically, the results of our policies succeeding and improving the lives of Singapore families.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: That is why I said tackling inequality is unfinished business.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: But I stress there is no contradiction between meritocracy and fairness, nor reducing inequality and raising our collective standards.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Instead, we should double up on meritocracy, by broadening its definition to embrace various talents and skills.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We should not cap achievement at the top, but work harder to lift the bottom.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: I wanted to set out these fundamentals, because it is important to have broad agreement around them.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: If we have, we are in a much better position to develop the education system to better prepare our children for the future.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: As to what exactly we need to do in terms of programmes, initiatives and policy reviews, MOE will take in all the views and suggestions raised inside and outside of this House and consider them.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Others may involve trade-offs and we may decide not to implement them for the time being.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: He asked, “What is the most important school you attend?

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Who are our most important teachers?” My answer is this: the most important school is our family; the most important teacher is our parents.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Of course, it takes a village to raise a child.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: But the home and the parents are one of the most important education experiences all of us would have.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Imagine a family is a school and a parent is a teacher.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Between the parent and the child, it is a complex relationship.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: All of us who are parents would know that there are expectations, love, respect, hopes, fears, and worries, as a parent.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: It is a complex relationship and MOE is in the middle of it.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: It also means that being an educator is a great privilege because you get to educate a child who is the most cherished and valuable to the parents.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: This is why Mr Darryl David mentioned that being a teacher is unlike all other professions, it is unlike a lawyer or a pilot, where nobody questions you on how you do your job.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: But when it comes to teachers, parents will question, because parents, too, are the most important teachers to the child.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: And it is a complex relationship between mother and child; father and child.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: There are so many opinions on education because of that.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: It is so close to our hearts because it affects the closest people in our lives – our children.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: It also means that discussions on education can be frustrating and sometimes end up in a stalemate.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Parents will say, "MOE, you better change." MOE will say, "I think parents, too, you need to change." Sometimes, we point fingers at each other.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: They look at you and say, "I think both of you better change." The truth is, we are all in this together, as partners, to build a better future.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: I feel optimistic and hopeful because, through all these speeches today, it may appear that we have different views.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: But underlying all that, there is consensus on the direction ahead.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: I do not think we ever had such a strong chorus of voices in the House, emphasising the importance of joy of learning and cautioning against excessive tuition and relentless chasing of academic results.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: I believe this is a view that will reverberate beyond this Chamber.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: MOE and all our partners will work together.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: All of us cannot fail the young people of Singapore and cannot fail our society.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Our commitment goes beyond our students in school to adult learners who have graduated from the formal school system.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: MOE leads the SkillsFuture movement, which emphasises opportunities for Singaporeans to fulfil their potential, regardless of starting points.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: A wide range of subsidised modular courses are available through the SkillsFuture series at our Institutes of Higher Learning (IHLs).

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: We also empower individuals to make informed decisions for lifelong learning through the MySkillsFuture portal, which hosts online self-assessment tools.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: This ensures that those who may have had a rockier start than most, can still find a path back into learning and retool themselves for a better future.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: For now, let us go back to the start of a child's educational journey.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: MOE believes that with a robust system of support, all children can go on to lead confident, independent lives with hope in the future.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: I will cover three points, specifically, how MOE is committed to investing in three groups of students: our students from disadvantaged families; our high-needs learners; and our students with special educational needs.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: First, I will talk about supporting our children from disadvantaged families.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Let us start with Sitihajar, who is currently a Primary 1 student at Riverside Primary School.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Prior to joining Riverside Primary School, she was enrolled in MK@Riverside in 2016.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: This has benefited children like Sitihajar, who may not have had the opportunity to enjoy quality and affordable preschool education otherwise.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Sitihajar also benefited from the subsidies provided through the Kindergarten Fee Assistance Scheme.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Sitihajar was also able to redeem three sets of uniforms yearly, as part of the Start-Up Grant of $240.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: While she joined MK@Riverside with fear and anxiety, Sitihajar blossomed into a confident and joyful learner.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Her experience at MOE Kindergarten gave her a good head start when she enrolled in Riverside Primary School this year.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Similarly, her brother, Saiful, who is in Primary 4 this year in the same school, also receives financial support under MOE's Financial Assistance Scheme.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Under this scheme, he has his school and miscellaneous fees waived and receives free textbooks, school attires and transport subsidies.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: He is automatically placed on the School Meals Programme, where he can use the meal subsidies for breakfast, lunch and recess.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: With basic needs, such as food and transportation, no longer a concern, Saiful is a friendly and helpful student who is fully engaged in his learning.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: I should add that MOE's financial assistance would apply to Saiful, even if his family is already receiving concurrent help from other agencies.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: We do not want financial concerns to prevent our children from exploring their interests.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Over the past few years, Saiful has been able to tap on the school's Opportunity Fund to enjoy co-curricular activities, such as a local learning journey to the River Safari.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: In the future, as Sitihajar and Saiful progress to a post-secondary educational institution, such as ITE, polytechnics or autonomous universities (AU), we will continue to support them.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Since 2017, we have increased the quantum and extended the coverage of Government bursaries for ITE, polytechnic and AU students.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: By raising the annual bursary quantum of the Community Development Council/Citizens Consultative Committee Bursary by between $200 to $400, depending on the institution, we can help students further defray the cost of post-secondary education.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: We have also enhanced students' access to these bursaries by introducing Gross Monthly Household Income as an alternative income assessment, so that more students qualify for assistance.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Students may also apply for other merit-based scholarships and financial assistance schemes offered by foundations, Self-Help Groups and other community or private organisations.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: More than 60% of our students in polytechnics and AUs receive similar support.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: So, just like Sitihajar and Saiful, other children with a similar background can be assured that they will be given the same opportunities, regardless of their family circumstances.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: I will speak now about investing in our high-needs learners and preparing all students for the future.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: MOE remains committed to helping our weaker students in schools through levelling-up initiatives.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: For example, additional teachers are provided to ensure that the Learning Support Programme and its sister programme, Learning Support for Mathematics, for lower primary students, are conducted in small groups of less than 10.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: A primary school student on these programmes would have received 60% more resourcing, compared to a peer not on the programme.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: At the secondary level, MOE provides additional resourcing for students from the Normal course.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: To smoothen their transition to post-secondary education, these students can take Elective Modules, which are 20- to 30-hour modules that secondary schools may develop together with our ITEs and polytechnics.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Bendemeer Secondary School is one such good school that has done well to support its students from the Normal course.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: As part of its Elective Module Framework, the school identifies accredited Science and Technology courses at ITE that would benefit students as they face the future economy.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: For Secondary 4 students, the Elective Modules are used as precursors for different pathways, leading to post-secondary education institutions.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: The support provided by Bendemeer Secondary School is not just academic.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: They also have the Students Overcome Adversity Responsibly (SOAR) programme, that engages at-risk youths after school.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Through the programme, these students engage in healthy and meaningful recreational activities jointly planned by community partners, such as Family Service Centres.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: MOE also provides authentic work-experience opportunities for students in Specialised Schools, such as NorthLight School and Assumption Pathway School.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: For students in these schools who are not yet ready to further their education at ITE or start work independently at the workplace, they can join the Work-Study Pathways programme.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: They will have on-the-job learning at the workplace for three days and continue with their education for the remaining two.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Regardless where our students begin in life, MOE has always placed importance on nurturing students who do not just have the mastery of knowledge, but also skills and attributes required to succeed in life.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: So, we look at the different strengths and we help them as much as we can.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Mr Azmoon Ahmad acknowledged the success of the Malay community and shared his concerns about children from disadvantaged backgrounds.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: He has concerns if they are able to progress as well as they should.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: (In Malay):  : 	Sir, there have been discussions on the state of the Malay community.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: One of the discussions is about the concern that we have not progressed, left behind and excluded from the nation’s development.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: So far, the Malay community has shown progress in education, as we will see from the data that I will be sharing now.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: We have also seen an increase in the number of students who have attained passes in three “O” level subjects.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: For "A" level students, 76.4% of students who sat for the examinations in 2007 have obtained passes in at least three H2 subjects, as well as passes in General Paper and Knowledge and Inquiry.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Our children have shown an improved performance currently.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: With an even higher passing rate, they have even more options when they continue their studies at the post-secondary level, including various opportunities for higher education and getting better jobs.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: However, as a community, there is still more that we can do.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: We must be aware of the needs of our neighbours, family members and friends by giving our support and encouragement to them.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: I will now continue my speech in English where I will touch on our efforts and support for our children with Special Education Needs.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: (In English): The last group of students I will focus on is our students with Special Educational Needs.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Ms Rahayu Mahzam earlier highlighted her experience as a parent of a child with special needs.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: The role of parents and caregivers is critical and a challenging one, especially during the crucial transition points of the care recipient's life.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: As the Senior Parliamentary Secretary for MSF, I would like to reassure Ms Rahayu Mahzam and Ms Chia Yong Yong that the Government has not forgotten families and caregivers of persons with disabilities.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: As part of our efforts under the Third Enabling Masterplan, we are adopting a whole-of-life approach to ensuring adequate support and transition for persons with disabilities and their caregivers at each life stage.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: MSF will develop a framework to support caregivers, especially new parents of children with special needs, to build relevant skills and improve their understanding of special needs.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: For young children at risk of developmental delays, the Government aims to strengthen early detection and intervention to maximise their developmental potential.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: MSF is piloting the development of a continuum of early intervention services with varying intensities, to better meet the different needs of our children over time.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: We hope that early intervention will give our children a good start as they progress to formal education.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: As we support our students, we recognise the need to change the narrative in our society.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: We want to celebrate our children, to focus on their abilities, not disabilities.
