speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: We want to work towards a society where we do not just accept, but embrace those who are differently-abled.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: We want to see this cultural change in our schools, both SPED and mainstream.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: The sense of welcome that we want to achieve has to be developed and achieved over time and with sustained effort.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: We need everyone to commit to this – teachers, schools, parents, the public, employers and the wider society.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Likewise, we have to teach our children with Special Educational Needs to be advocates for themselves.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: They must learn how to communicate their needs to friends, co-workers and employers and to be confident contributors to our society.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: MOE recognises the importance of skills development for all our students with Special Educational Needs.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Sometimes, these skills are best developed in customised learning environments, such as small groups, so that students with particular learning needs can receive intensive learning experiences.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Sometimes, the skills need to be developed in authentic "real world" contexts, such as the experience of communicating with typically developing peers and adults in community settings.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: This is because not all our students with Special Educational Needs are comfortable in social settings and require a long-term level of support by specially-trained teachers to develop the skills needed.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: The best combination of both settings – customised and "real world" – varies from child to child.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: A child who has moderate to severe needs will benefit from extensive support available in SPED schools and a paced inclusion in "real world" settings, through interaction opportunities with peers and adults in a variety of activities.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: A child with mild Special Educational Needs can function in the typical settings of a mainstream school's lessons and CCAs but will need occasional pull out sessions, perhaps once a week, one-to-one or in a small group, to learn certain skills more explicitly.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: This is where we are seeking to have a hybrid approach.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: The learning environment of a SPED school accommodates the needs of such students, allowing them to learn at a comfortable pace.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: When they are ready, they have opportunities to interact with peers in other schools, such as through the Satellite Partnerships.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Internationally, school systems continue to wrestle with the question of what is the right amount of inclusion for students with Special Educational Needs.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Ms Chia Yong Yong and Ms Rahayu Mahzam have shared with us approaches to inclusion which need to be studied further.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: They spend a large portion of their day learning together with their peers.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: This is where they attend the mainstream schools.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: All schools have a core group of teachers, known as our Teachers Trained in Special Needs, to provide support to students in our classrooms.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: We recognise the importance of equipping our teachers with these skills and have stepped up our efforts to train more in the next few years.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Our Allied Educators in Learning and Behavioural Support also work alongside our teachers.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Because of Autism Spectrum Disorder, Sam had difficulties approaching teachers and presenting in class.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: He would feel sick and look for opportunities to avoid these situations.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: This is unfortunate, because while Sam has a flair for Chinese orchestral music and plays the "Ruan" well, he is afraid of performing in front of others.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Thankfully, we have an Allied Educator, Mr Lae Chung Kit, who worked closely with Sam's teachers and parent, to equip Sam with the strategies to manage his anxiety-related difficulties in social situations.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Eventually, I am happy to share, Sam applied what he learnt and put up a great performance in front of the whole school!

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: We know that there are many more teachers and Allied Educators like Mr Lae out there who are supporting our students to overcome their learning difficulties.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: A number of students in mainstream schools also need support for other physical impairments or for hearing loss or visual impairment.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: MOE fully funds a range of Assistive Technological Devices, also known as AT Devices, for them and also collaborates with two Volunteer Welfare Organisations, the Asian Women's Welfare Association and The Singapore Association for the Deaf, to provide integration and learning support for students with physical and sensory impairments.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: These organisations also provide training for students and teachers on the use of AT Devices.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Likewise, students in SPED schools who need AT Devices receive them for free.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: I have shared Sam's journey in a mainstream school.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Now, I would like to share the story of Emeth, who graduated from MINDS Woodlands Gardens School in 2017.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Job coaches supported him at various work experiences organised by the school and its industry partners.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Emeth's parents also worked with the school to reinforce his travel training skills and build his stamina and fitness for employment.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: This year, Emeth found employment at the Yishun Community Hospital, in the Kitchen Department, where he works as a Kitchen Attendant.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: They are employed in diverse sectors, such as healthcare, homes, retail and hospitality.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: By 2019, we hope to expand this programme from the current 12 SPED schools, to 15.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Members have asked whether students like Sam and Emeth get to meet with other students and how well they and their peers are doing in interacting with and understanding one another.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Mainstream students are learning important lessons on empathy and acceptance of others who are different from them.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: This includes explicit instruction about the needs of Persons with Disabilities through the Character and Citizenship Education syllabus.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Our schools have also developed programmes to strengthen peer support, so that no child is left behind.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: The Rainbow Peer Support Leaders Programme by Orchid Park Secondary School does just that.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Students who have been identified to be part of the programme are taught how to support their classmates with Special Educational Needs.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: They become advocates for their peers, sharing and standing up for them in classrooms.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Admittedly, some schools have gone further along the road to an inclusive culture through these programmes, but it is something that every school is committed to bringing about.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Our Satellite Partnership programme has been the bridge in linking our students from both SPED and mainstream schools.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: As we see our SPED students grow in confidence through the programme, we see our mainstream students grow in empathy.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: However, partnerships and activities are not limited to the Satellite Partnership.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: At the recent Singapore Youth Festival Concert, students rehearsed and performed alongside each other in a range of items.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: The upcoming National Day Celebrations will also bring both groups of students together.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: This partnership allows for Pathlight students to be taught by Pathlight teachers in self-contained satellite classes sited within mainstream schools.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Where appropriate, Pathlight School students join their mainstream peers in their classes for academic learning.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: This model is possible because the academic and social inclusion opportunities serve the needs of the Pathlight students.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: The experience is, however, not easy for these students with moderate autism.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Yet, gradual exposure over a period of years have benefited these students who go on to post-secondary education institutes.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: We have also extended our range of Special Educational Needs support in post-secondary education institutes, as our students with special educational needs move on to the next stage of their education.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: This is a one-stop support unit where students, such as Benjamin, can seek support as they chase their dreams.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Benjamin is currently a second-year student with visual impairment, studying for his Diploma in Electrical and Electronics Engineering at Singapore Polytechnic.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: The SSO also arranged for Benjamin to visit the Resource Centre at the Singapore Association of the Visually Handicapped, so he could find the best AT Device for his needs.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: He eventually chose a handheld device which makes reading easier by enlarging fonts and adjusting the colour contrast of materials.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: With the support of his lecturers, friends and staff from the SSO, Benjamin has been doing very well.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: As I mentioned earlier, we want to see a change in our schools, both SPED and mainstream – one where our children are celebrated and accepted, where we focus on their strengths and abilities to help them reach their potential.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Have we got the balance right between the customised settings in our SPED schools and the amount of interaction opportunities afforded by Satellite Partnerships today?

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: I think we have made progress, but we still have ways to go.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: As I see the passion and the concerted efforts of the teachers in both SPED and mainstream schools and also the passion and the touching words and what was spoken earlier, I am confident such inclusion efforts will gain momentum.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: In our schools, we must teach our students to be empathetic and accepting of people who are differently-abled from us, who learn at a different pace from us and who come from different family backgrounds from us.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: From the stories I have shared today, it is heartening to see that we are building students of character.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: While we are continuously improving the affordability, accessibility and quality of educational support provisions to students, as adults in the world of work and society, we must be sensitive to the needs of every Singaporean.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: We must welcome and support them, regardless of their background and starting point in life.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: In other words, where we begin in life will not dictate where we end up.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: I would also like to thank Ms Rahayu Mahzam for her amendments which help to flesh out how we should do this and provides the frame for the action plan, as well as all the Members who have spoken and contributed to this debate.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Listening to the speeches, there are some key themes that have emerged.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The first is that parents want reassurance that their children will have a bright future and that they will not lose out.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: We have heard much about a future-ready education system, stress, competition, the PSLE, lifelong learning, inclusivity.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: All these are really different aspects of the same concern, which is, trying to ensure that our children have the best possible chance to succeed.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Second, even as we want our children to get ahead, there is also a strong sentiment that we want our children to be able to enjoy their years in school.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Mr Louis Ng, Mr Darryl David and Mr Kok Heng Leun spoke about this.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: We do not want the children's years in school to be only about homework, tests, assessments, grades and examination scores.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Schooling must also be an enjoyable educational experience, built around a love of learning, of exploration and of play.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: It must be holistic, teaching skills like critical thinking, to prepare them for the new world ahead and it must have the emotional well-being of students at heart.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Mr Ganesh Rajaram and Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin also spoke about the need to change our culture, that as teachers, parents, as a society, we need to give our children space to grow.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: We need to listen to them better in order to support them better.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Third, many of you also spoke about how this love of learning must be a lifelong one.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Ms Thanaletchmi, Assoc Prof Randolph Tan and Mr Darryl David urged that our children must continue to learn after they leave school and throughout their working lives.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Employees and employers alike must be nimble and receptive to on-the-job training.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Many Members of Parliament, including Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan, Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin and Mr Azmoon Ahmad raised the issue of inequality.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: You worry that the vulnerable, the disabled and the low-income will not be able to get as much out of the education system as those who are better off, that they will get left behind and that the gap is widening.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: This shows that, as a people, we care about those who are disadvantaged.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: A fifth common theme was that of inclusivity, integration and social mixing.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Ms Rahayu Mahzam, Ms Chia Yong Yong and Mr Henry Kwek have spoken passionately about this.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: We are concerned that children born with special needs will go through life without being embraced or valued by society.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: We are concerned that the divide between rich and poor or between children from different backgrounds and communities may grow.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: This is important because it says something about our values and the kind of society we want, the kind of people that we are, and we want a society that is more equal, more unified.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Lastly, a call for us to work together to achieve these goals.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Ms Denise Phua spoke about the need for the Government to tap on the ideas, expertise of stakeholders to develop policies and programmes together, as we shape an education system for the future.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: On all these broad objectives, we are aligned.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: We, too, want every child to have a bright future and to do well.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Like Members of Parliament who have spoken, we want them to have a wonderful school experience.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: We are also concerned about the vulnerable and we want integration and inclusivity to be at the heart of our education system.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Minister Ong Ye Kung and Senior Parliamentary Secretary Faishal Ibrahim have already explained some of our Ministry's programmes and the considerations behind our work.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: So, let me wrap up MOE's response by sharing with the House where we are coming from in terms of the big picture: our mission, what we have done, what we are doing and what we will be doing.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Every day, many vehicles and pedestrians go past the MOE signage along North Buona Vista Road.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: It is a mission we take very seriously.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: MOE has walked a life journey, not just with the nation, but also with every Singaporean who has passed through the education system.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: When Singapore achieved Independence in 1965, Mdm Iris Wong was 11 years old.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: She used to walk in the hot sun to May South Primary School.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: School was often disrupted because of social unrest and racial riots.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Our priority for a newly independent country was mass education for a young population and to help people get jobs in an era of industrialisation.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: She began work in her father's tailoring shop and had three children, one of whom was a daughter, Josephine.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Josephine went to Outram Primary in the 1980s.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: She drank milk out of little plastic packets and brushed her teeth over the school drain – as I did when I went to primary school in the 1970s!

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: In the 1970s, we had milk, too, because milk was to help children get strong bones as rickets was still a problem at that time, due to poor nutrition in a country that was still not well-off.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: We were moving up the value chain, from a lower-skill manufacturing base, which was producing things like fish hooks and matches, to a more capital-intensive and a high-skills economy, producing electronics and petrochemicals.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The education system had to adapt to equip Singaporeans to thrive in this new situation and also to address high dropout rates.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: That was when streaming was introduced to cater to our children's different learning paces.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The school dropout rate fell sharply after streaming.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Josephine left school, went to polytechnic, worked for a few years and then she got a degree in Marketing Communications.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: By the time she was being courted by her husband-to-be sometime in the 2000s, the education system was coming of age and undergoing a paradigm shift.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: We had entered the phase of the knowledge-based economy, where ideas and information are the key drivers of growth.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: We also gave our schools greater autonomy to be innovative in programmes and invested in Information and Communications Technology.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: To deliver this, we hired more teachers and strengthened teachers' professional development to improve teaching quality.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: In 2010, Josephine gave birth to a beautiful baby girl, Vera.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: She started primary school in CHIJ Toa Payoh last year.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The future that she faces will be very different from that of her grandmother and her mother.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The beginning of this decade when she was born marked the end of the Global Financial Crisis and the beginning of what we call the future economy.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The future economy calls for a very different sort of education from that undertaken by Iris and Josephine.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: It will be a VUCA environment – Volatile, Uncertain, Complex, Ambiguous.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: It is a future driven by the need for skills, innovation, adaptability and flexibility.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: It will see the weight of the global economy shift towards Asia.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Members have correctly identified that our education system needs to be able to respond to this.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: And, in fact, MOE has already embarked on this.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: We are undertaking a transformational change for the next phase in our development.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The reason that I went through this history of MOE is really to show that, at each stage, as times changed, MOE has responded, our education system has responded.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: It has adapted and adjusted in order to walk that journey with the nation and with Singaporeans.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Now, it is really about developing each individual and creating multiple pathways.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: First, we now put a lot more emphasis on developing the whole child, not just their academic achievements.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: This is key to our student-centric, values-driven philosophy.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: I know people do not like jargons like "student-centric", but, basically, what it means is we put the child at the centre of it and we build around that.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: MOE's approach is actually best reflected in our 21st Century Competency Framework.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: I have asked the Clerks to put copies of this on Members' seats.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: You may see it and if I could ask you to refer to it.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: It is often referred to as the MOE Swiss Roll but I think if we want to be technically correct, it should be an Arctic roll; Baby Boomers will know which ice-cream I am referring to.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: If you look at it, you will see that the core of the framework is values, because at the end of the day, the most important thing is, for the individuals, what kind of person you are, your character.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: So, values are at the core of it.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: And this ties in with Character and Citizenship Development, which we have made as a central part of our education system.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The next two rings reflect the social and emotional skills that our children will need to navigate the world ahead; and the outermost ring shows what kind of people we eventually want them to be: confident, able to learn on their own, contributing actively in all their undertakings to society and to be good citizens.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: So, for the Members who have spoken about the need for character, for good attributes, please be assured that this is actually a focus of our education system.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Next, we have to ensure that our children will attain knowledge, to have a solid foundation in literacy and numeracy.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: But this book knowledge alone is not enough.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: This year, OECD published a paper entitled "Education 2030: The Future of Education and Skills".

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Future-ready students will need broad knowledge, but also practical skills, like the ability to utilise new technology.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: These skills will be in great demand by employers.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The ability to learn, unlearn and relearn will be key.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Much of the stress that we have talked about is really driven by the assumption that there is only one path to success – the academic route.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: This has led to the fear that if children do not get into certain schools or into the Express stream, then they will not have a bright future.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: However, there are, in fact, many different paths to success.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Different children have different personalities, talents and abilities.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Others are much better with their hands or are more creative and artistic.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: And different children respond differently to different methods of teaching.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The future economy will be much more diverse than today's.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Doctors, lawyers, engineers, architects and accountants will still be around, but the way they do their jobs will be very different.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: There will be increased demand for jobs in new areas like Financial Technology, Data Analytics, Artificial Intelligence and Virtual Reality.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: And yet, it is our task to prepare her for it, for a job that we do not even know is going to come into existence yet.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: And for that, you cannot have a system that is one-size-fits-all, nor is there any longer a single measure of success.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: In recognition of this, we have, over the years, introduced different types of schools and programmes to cater for the different strengths and talents of different individuals.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: We have the usual "O" and "A" level route, but we also have established the Integrated Programme in various schools to give students more time to immerse themselves in broader learning experiences.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: We have the Sports School to cater for sporting talent, School of The Arts for those artistically inclined; we have the NUS High School of Math and Science for those who are Science, Technology, Engineeering and Mathematics (STEM)-inclined; and the School of Science and Technology which focuses on STEM as well, but their curriculum also centres on applied and interdisciplinary learning.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Then we have Crest and Spectra Secondary Schools to cater to students who would benefit from a skills-based, hands-on curriculum.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: There is Northlight and Assumption Pathway to cater for those who may otherwise be at risk of leaving school prematurely.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: We have secondary schools with Enhanced Art and Music programmes.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Mr Kok Heng Leun spoke passionately about Arts and the Humanities.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: I would encourage Mr Kok and all Members here to visit the Singapore Youth Festival Art Exhibition which is just next door at the National Gallery.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: You would be amazed at the quality of some of the artwork that is being produced by our students.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: More recently, we have introduced Applied Learning Programmes (ALP) in all secondary schools.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Changkat Changi Secondary School, whose programme, aptly entitled "SOAR", partners aviation industry giants to give students opportunities to deepen their understanding of aeronautics.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: And Teck Whye Primary School, where students are introduced to Design Thinking concepts, using 3D printing technologies to bring their projects to life.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: We have adjusted the system for different aptitudes and paces of learning.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: So, in its place, we introduced differentiated learning, which recognises that different children have different strengths and also learn different subjects at different paces.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: This is the subject-based banding, where students can take combinations of standard and foundation subjects.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: At secondary school, the Express, Normal (Academic) and Normal (Technical) streams cater to the different talents, strengths and abilities of our students.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: We have now also extended	subject-based banding to cover both the lower and upper secondary levels.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: We also have many more subjects and many more subject combinations.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Students can dabble in Food and Consumer Education, stand at work benches filling in with different ingredients, instead of at their usual desks; or they can take China Studies to learn about the complexities of Chinese society.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: In our IHLs, we now also have subjects which were unknown to parents when they were in school.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Singapore Polytechnic’s Diploma in Perfumery and Cosmetic Science taps into a growing global market for fragrance products.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: At least five of the world’s top flavour and fragrance houses are now based in Singapore and these students’ skills will be highly valued.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: ITE offers a Higher Nitec in Games Art and Design where you can learn how to create unforgettable characters and entire virtual worlds!

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: And our students are so good, they create games that end up being finalists in showcases like the Tokyo Game Show (TGS).

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: In addition to all of these, we have created multiple pathways to success.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Post-secondary, we now have the ITE with three campuses, five polytechnics and six AUs.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: When students graduate, they can continue to learn, making use of their SkillsFuture credits, or enrol in part-time courses for adults.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Traditional universities like National University of Singapore and Nanyang Technological University, based on the British model, or Singapore Management University – which is more a US-style business school.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: In the last few years, we have added three new publicly-funded universities – the Singapore University of Technology and Design (SUTD) for engineering, computing, and architecture; the Singapore Institute of Technology (SIT) for science and technology; and the Singapore University of Social Sciences (SUSS) for the social sciences.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: And SIT and SUSS have a more applied pedagogy and curriculum.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: There are many different ways to reach an ultimate goal.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: You can go the academic route from secondary to JC to university; or to polytechnic, then work; or attend ITE and work through the Work-Learn Technical Diploma; or go to ITE, then polytechnic, then university; or go to polytechnic, work and then move on to university or other professional certifications.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: We have made SkillsFuture a movement for lifelong learning, supported by the many SkillsFuture Programmes under MOE, as well as the Adapt and Grow Programmes under MOM.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: This means that adults can secure places in diploma courses through course-specific talents, because the polytechnics will better recognise work experience, instead of relying only on academic results.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: This is yet another example of our commitment to ensuring that people have many opportunities to progress.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: That said, we do acknowledge that there are concerns about over-drilling and an over-emphasis on grades.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: We, on our part, have made moves to reduce PSLE stress.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: We stopped revealing the top PSLE scores; we removed banding of schools by academic results.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: This will reduce fine differentiation and comparison between students.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: It means more schools will share the same cut-off points.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: We will also introduce tie-breakers – choice, for example – that are not related to academic results.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Senior Parliamentary Secretary Faishal Ibrahim has addressed this.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: But let me just affirm that this is an area in which we want to provide the best possible support to those with special needs and will continue to be an important part of our work.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Ms Chia Yong Yong spoke very passionately just now on this topic.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: To Ms Chia, I would like to say that she is definitely not a burden.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: In fact, she is very much a blessing.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Her disability or, rather, special ability, has enabled her to give this House insights and perspectives that we would not otherwise have had and this has enriched our debate and informed our policy, and her presence here has given us much more positive contributions.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: This is the value and the benefit of inclusivity and being able to draw on people with different talents and abilities.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: We will continue to ensure that education remains an integrating force that brings everyone together.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: On the joy of learning, many Members spoke about this and the importance of giving students time and space to discover who they are.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: We share their concerns about a culture of over-drilling and over-testing.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Nurturing a love for learning in our students is equally important to us.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: We start early – from the preschool years.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Our Nurturing Early Learners curriculum, as Mr Louis Ng pointed out, recognises the importance of purposeful play.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: This framework is shared with the entire preschool sector.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The Early Childhood Development Agency’s regulations have also placed more emphasis on outdoor play and physical development.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: We have taken steps to unlock curiosity and encourage the joy of learning in our teaching pedagogies, for example, our Programmes for Active Learning and learning through "unstructured" play, where children can engage in open-ended and free play.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: In Punggol Primary, teachers set up stations full of supplies for children – nets, leaves, twigs – to create their own rules and games.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: At Yang Zheng Primary, students learn English through performing and dramatising stories together.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: We are facilitating sharing among educators on how to adopt innovative and engaging teaching practices so students will enjoy learning through initiatives like the Singapore Teaching Practice, an online portal for teachers.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: We acknowledge sentiments from the public, from the House, about how we can work to free our students from the never-ending worksheets and tests.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: For example, Keming Primary School is exploring moving away from Common Tests, which used to take up about three weeks of curriculum time, to regular checkpoint assessments instead, so that more time is freed up for other learning experiences.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: MOE’s Director-General of Education, Mr Wong Siew Hoong, recently sent a note around to the fraternity.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: In it, he affirmed the good work of teachers.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: He also encouraged everyone to adopt a spirit of introspection, to reflect on whether some of our practices, despite being done out of love for the child, may have unintended consequences.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: For example, by giving them too many tests which may deprive them of time for other activities.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: So, we will do our part, but we do need the parents and other stakeholders to do their part, too.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Mr Louis Ng called for a review of performance-based ranking for teachers, because he was concerned that they might teach for the test.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Teachers are assessed on a wide range of criteria: quality teaching and learning; character development of students; professional development of self and others; and demonstrated desired personal attributes, professional values and ethics, content mastery and pedagogy of instruction.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Members have also expressed concerns about students who are less well-off and disadvantaged.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: We pay a lot of attention to this group, with interventions and financial assistance.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: This has enabled students from disadvantaged backgrounds to do better.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: We also top the world in the Trends in International Mathematics and Science Study (TIMSS) – in mathematics and science.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: We are number two in the world in the Progress in International Reading Literacy Study (PIRLS).

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: What this shows us is, there are high peaks.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: We have one of the highest proportions of students performing at the highest levels of proficiency: about one-third to half of our students.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan asked if this means that our Singaporean students are ready for the brave new world.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The fact that our students come out tops in collaborative problem-solving is promising because it measures not just their content knowledge, but their ability to work with others, communicate and solve complex problems.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: What this means is that our schools are supporting students from all socio-economic backgrounds to do well and that they do better than their peers in other countries.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Nevertheless, like Members who have spoken today, we, too, are concerned about the widening income gap even as the middle class are uplifted and do better over time.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The solution is to uplift those at the lower end and close the gap without chopping the top and holding back those who do well, as Minister Ong Ye Kung said just now.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: This is something we are committed to do.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: I also want to say what drives much of our work to support and uplift students are our committed educators, who are at the heart of the system.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: It is our educators who motivate students and who identify opportunities for them.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: For example, Outram Secondary School has a remarkable principal, Mr Boo Hian Kok.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: He formed a task force, consisting of teachers and Student Welfare Officers, to address Long-Term Absentee cases, the children who did not turn up for school.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: For those teachers, their calendar is cleared for the first few periods in the morning.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: If students do not turn up by 8.00 am, these teachers will make phone calls, visit homes, knock on their doors and encourage the families to send them to school.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The task force makes a special effort to understand and empathise with the family’s difficulties.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: They build rapport, so that the family trusts that the school has their child’s welfare at heart.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: And this has helped many students like Jimmy, not his real name, feel welcome and safe.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: He used to skip school because his stepmother has a chronic illness and he had to buy her meals.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: With the school’s help, he now stays with his grandparents, who are better able to care for him.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: He loves soccer, so, the school placed him in a special soccer programme to encourage him to come back.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: At the end of the day, you can see that all of us – parents, teachers, MOE – want the same thing.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: We want our children and our people to do well.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: We want them to have as enjoyable an education as possible and we want them to enjoy learning.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The key is in striking the right balance and having the right mindset.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: On balance, Mr Louis Ng called on us to de-emphasise academic content and emphasise play and exploration.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: At the same time, Assoc Prof Randolph Tan cautioned that "the last thing we want to do is for everyone to discard the foundations currently offered by our education system" and that "having a solid foundation in the basics also prepares them for self-directed learning throughout the rest of their lifelong journey as a learner." So, both of them have slightly different perspectives but are on the same spectrum.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The question is, where do you set the balance?

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: And that is MOE's task; and that is what MOE strives to do.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: We have already embarked on the shifts which embody much of what Members have called for.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: We are not removing PSLE, but the transformation is still taking place as we move more to Applied Learning.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The process is ongoing and we do welcome the ideas and suggestions that have been put forward by Members today.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Ms Denise Phua called for a committee to develop an education master plan.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The form that this takes is perhaps not so critical, but the key thrust of her suggestion is that achieving our education objectives is really a partnership between all stakeholders.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: But mindset is a difficult thing to change.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: And we call on all partners to do this.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: As I was reading the newspapers today, I flipped to the Forum page and I saw a letter written by a young, 17-year-old JC student, Teo Chen Wei.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: We want excellence, but excellence does not mean excellence purely in academic grades alone.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: There are many other paths, as I have pointed out.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: So, you could be excellent in aeronautics, or the culinary arts.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Whatever it is, we want excellence because we want our people to do well.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: At the same time, does failure mean that you cannot progress?

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The answer is no, because we have created so many different pathways and we hope that people will see a setback as something from which to learn and to move forward.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: But, as I have explained earlier, there are many different paths and I would really urge parents and students to explore what is available and to choose the option that is right for a particular individual.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: There is a group of parents who started the campaign “Life Beyond Grades” to demonstrate that the path to success does not depend on grades alone.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Parenting is one of the toughest but most fulfilling roles and they all just want the best for their children.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: So, I hope that more people would adopt this kind of a mindset.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Our system has enabled people to rise from disadvantaged circumstances and to do well.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan
text: I say this because I think we have been very fortunate.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan
text: We have had Ms Rahayu Mahzam suggest amendments to the original Motion, which we actually accepted consensually.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan
text: And we have also had three Members of the Government respond.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan
text: We have had Minister Ong Ye Kung speak about the paradoxes which I will mention in a moment.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan
text: We have Senior Parliamentary Secretary Faishal Ibrahim talk about what is being done for the disadvantaged and disabled communities, or the vulnerable groups.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan
text: And we have had a wrap-up by Second Minister Indranee Rajah.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan
text: What I will say, Mr Deputy Speaker, is that I think what has been best put forward — I mean, all of us have spoken about these issues and we have agreed on a lot of those points.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan
text: But what has come out, which I think is refreshing in some ways, is that the Government has heard what we have been speaking about.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan
text: And the Ministry has come forward to say that there are areas where the imperfections are there.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan
text: The education system is being tweaked as we speak.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan
text: I found out just 10 minutes ago what the transformation plan that the Ministry of Education (MOE) has in mind and I think Ms Denise Phua will also be very happy to hear about this.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan
text: If this is what we have, if this is what we are looking at, I think we have a bright future in terms of the future of education.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan
text: The first is there has to be a move away from the stalemate between parents and the education system.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan
text: This is also problematic because a lot of system designers within MOE are also parents.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan
text: So, I think the first point that has to be made and that has been made by the three Government speakers earlier, is that everyone acknowledges that stress is there.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan
text: Everyone acknowledges that the children, or the young persons, or the students are dealing with this stress.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan
text: How do we alleviate these problems without sacrificing excellence and meritocracy?

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan
text: That has to be at the core of this.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan
text: The second point that I would like to make is that perhaps when we look at these points, moving away from the stalemate and, in fact, the acknowledgements that the PSLE and other systems are imperfect, is that not every sacred cow needs to be sacrificed.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan
text: I accept this because, partly, as a Hindu, I do not believe in cow sacrifice at all.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan
text: But perhaps, some aspects of the sacred PSLE need to be put out to pasture.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan
text: But I think parents generally, Singaporean parents, are wondering what will really differ so that I do not have to go and pay all my money to a tuition teacher.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan
text: That is really the question here; I think that is where it is going to go.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan
text: With that, Mr Deputy Speaker, I beg to move.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: Mr Kok Heng Leun, you have already made your speech, but I will allow you to seek a clarification if you make it brief.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun
text: My problem with PSLE is more of it happening at the age of 12.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun
text: For children at that age, going through that experience can be quite traumatic.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun
text: I understand the need for national examinations so that we know, we can allow students to, up to some point, be assessed and then, find the kind of things that they want to go for.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun
text: Is it possible that we consider, like in some other Scandinavian countries whereby basic education should last more than six years?

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun
text: It can start from six to 16 and, during that process, especially when we have this 21st Century Transformation Plan, where there is so much content in there, that, within those six years or even more and when there are examinations and national examinations in between, the process of learning actually cannot be deep enough.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun
text: Because you will be moving from learning a bit to preparing for examinations.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun
text: And I think perhaps the Ministry should start thinking about – that, in the long run, that we should have this shift.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun
text: The second thing is about play which fellow Members have talked about, purposeful play.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun
text: It is just scary that every play becomes purposeful.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun
text: Sometimes, whimsical play is equally important because it is only when it is whimsical, that we actually make greater discovery.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: We will certainly encourage our teachers and remind them of that.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: We do not want to dismantle something which really helps us to channel the students to the further path ahead.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: But I think the point that Mr Kok Heng Leun is really making is that, prior to age 12, or leading up to age 12, you want them to enjoy their learning; you want them to have enough content that they have a solid foundation; you do not want them to have so much stress that, not only do they not enjoy it, but it really becomes self-defeating in terms of the educational purpose.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: So, as I have said earlier, on those broad objectives, we are aligned.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: So, as we have said, we will work together on this.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: And, in fact, as Members have said, there is much hope, we are working to transform the system so that our students can be ready for the future.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: We look forward to working with Members, parents, teachers, educators in accomplishing this purpose.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: We have come to the conclusion of the debate.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: The original Motion, as amended, is now before the House.
